Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation

Minchan Jeong ††thanks: The two authors contributed equally to this work.††thanks: Work done while a Ph.D. student at KAIST. Affiliation: Center for AI and Natural Sciences, KIAS, Seoul 02455, South Korea Email: mailto:mcjeong@kias.re.krmcjeong@kias.re.kr    J. Jon Ryu ††thanks: Work done while a postdoctoral researcher at MIT. Affiliation: Department of CSE, Penn State University, University Park, PA 16802, USA Email: mailto:jongha@psu.edujongha@psu.edu    Se-Young Yun Affiliation: Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI, KAIST, Daejeon 34141, South Korea Email: mailto:yunseyoung@kaist.ac.kryunseyoung@kaist.ac.kr    Gregory W. Abstract

The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule’s electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need KK Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the KK ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires K2K^{2} Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-KK variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest KK eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at K=10K=10, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

1 Introduction

Ab initio quantum chemistry aims to compute the electronic states of molecules by solving the Schrödinger equation ℋ​ψ=ℰ​ψ\mathpzc{H}\psi=E\psi. Accurate computation of these states remains challenging due to the curse of dimensionality: the wavefunction lives on the 3​n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}-dimensional configuration space of n𝖾𝗅{n_{\mathsf{el}}} electrons, and the computational cost of traditional high-accuracy methods grows steeply with n𝖾𝗅{n_{\mathsf{el}}}. Recently, neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has emerged as a promising alternative, achieving chemical accuracy for the ground states of small molecules with architectures such as FermiNet [26], PauliNet [10], and Psiformer [38]. However, extending this success to excited states remains challenging. While minimizing the Rayleigh quotient naturally characterizes the ground state, computing multiple excited states requires an additional mechanism to recover mutually orthogonal eigenfunctions and identify their energy ordering. Moreover, such a mechanism must be compatible with VMC, where optimization relies on Monte Carlo samples drawn from the Born densities of the neural-network ansatzes.

Existing excited-state VMC methods can be broadly categorized into two approaches. On the one hand, penalty-based methods [3, 23, 39, 37] minimize the sum of the Rayleigh quotients of multiple ansatzes, augmented with penalties on their pairwise overlaps to encourage orthogonality. While conceptually straightforward, these methods require careful tuning of the penalty weights. In particular, Wheeler et al. [39] show that recovering the desired eigenstates at the global minimum requires sufficiently large penalty weights relative to the energy gaps, which are themselves unknown quantities to be estimated. On the other hand, natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) [27] takes an elegant, penalty-free approach by transforming the excited-state problem into a ground-state problem of an extended quantum system. By constructing a determinant from the individual ansatzes, NES-VMC implicitly enforces orthogonality without additional regularization. The individual eigenstates are then recovered by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian projected onto the learned subspace. However, this construction increases computational cost: evaluating its local energy requires K2K^{2} Laplacian evaluations per optimization step for KK states, compared to KK for penalty-based methods. Thus, the existing approaches present a tradeoff between penalty tuning and computational efficiency (Table 1).

We pursue a different variational perspective based on the low-rank approximation (LoRA) principle. Specifically, we build on NestedLoRA [30], a general framework for learning ordered eigenfunctions of an operator using neural networks, without explicitly imposing orthogonality constraints or introducing penalty weights. This framework has been successfully applied to low-dimensional partial differential equations and representation learning [30], as well as stochastic dynamical systems [14]. Despite these appealing properties, the LoRA objective is not directly compatible with VMC. The main obstacle is that it depends on the norms of the learned functions, which involve high-dimensional integrals that cannot be directly estimated from samples of their normalized Born densities.

Contributions.

We overcome this obstacle through a simple reparameterization, representing each function in the LoRA objective as a normalized neural-network ansatz multiplied by a trainable scale. This makes the resulting objective compatible with the Born sampling used in VMC. Building on this formulation, we propose NestedLoRA-VMC, which learns eigenstates directly in energy order through the sequential nesting technique [7, 30]. The proposed framework is penalty-free, requires no post-training diagonalization, and retains the global optimality characterization of the underlying LoRA principle. Moreover, NestedLoRA-VMC requires only KK Laplacian evaluations per optimization step, matching the cost of penalty-based methods rather than the K2K^{2} evaluations of NES-VMC. We evaluate NestedLoRA-VMC on first-row atoms from Li to Ne with K=10K=10 states and demonstrate accuracy comparable to NES-VMC and the state-of-the-art penalty-based method of Szabó et al. [37], without requiring gap-dependent penalty weights.

Organization.

Section 2 introduces the problem and existing excited-state VMC approaches. Section 3 develops the proposed VMC-compatible LoRA formulation and its theoretical properties. Section 4 presents experimental results, and Section 5 concludes with limitations and future directions. Proofs and additional technical details are deferred to the appendix.

2 Preliminaries

Our goal is to recover the KK lowest eigenpairs {(φk,Ek)}k=1K\{(\varphi_{k},E_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K} of the electronic Hamiltonian ℋ\mathpzc{H} of a molecule on the space ℋ\mathscr{H} of its wavefunctions, both defined below. We order them as E1≤E2≤⋯≤EKE_{1}\leq E_{2}\leq\cdots\leq E_{K}. Consider a molecule with n𝖾𝗅{n_{\mathsf{el}}} electrons at positions 𝐫1,…,𝐫n𝖾𝗅∈ℝ3\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and n𝗇𝗎{n_{\mathsf{nu}}} fixed nuclei of charges ZIZ_{I} at positions 𝐑I\mathbf{R}_{I}, I∈[n𝗇𝗎]I\in[{n_{\mathsf{nu}}}]. In the Born–Oppenheimer approximation and with 𝐱=(𝐫1,…,𝐫n𝖾𝗅){\bf x}=(\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{n_{\mathsf{el}}}), the non-relativistic electronic Hamiltonian is

ℋ:=∑𝒾=1𝓃𝖾𝗅{−12∇𝐫𝒾2−∑ℐ=1𝓃𝗇𝗎𝒵ℐ‖𝐫𝒾−𝐑ℐ‖}+∑1≤𝒾<𝒿≤𝓃𝖾𝗅1‖𝐫𝒾−𝐫𝒿‖,\mathpzc{H}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\biggl\{-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{2}-\sum_{I=1}^{n_{\mathsf{nu}}}\frac{Z_{I}}{\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}\|}\biggr\}+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}\frac{1}{\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}\|},

and the time-independent Schrödinger equation reads ℋ​ψ=ℰ​ψ\mathpzc{H}\psi=E\psi. Each electron also has a spin, up or down. We fix the numbers n↑n_{\uparrow} and n↓n_{\downarrow} of spin-up and spin-down electrons and assign the spins to the electrons, so that a wavefunction is a function of 𝐱{\bf x} alone that must be antisymmetric under exchange of two electrons with the same spin (Appendix D.1.1). The neural-network architecture enforces this antisymmetry (Appendix H.1). The wavefunctions therefore live in the space ℋ\mathscr{H} of complex-valued functions in L2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}) with this antisymmetry. As a closed subspace of L2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}), ℋ\mathscr{H} is a Hilbert space with the standard inner product ⟨fg⟩:=∫f∗(𝐱)g(𝐱)d𝐱\langle f~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~g\rangle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\int f^{*}({\bf x})g({\bf x})\,d{\bf x}. Since ℋ\mathpzc{H} commutes with permutations of same-spin electrons, it maps ℋ\mathscr{H} into itself. It is moreover self-adjoint on ℋ\mathscr{H}, a property that requires its adjoint to have the same domain and that the Kato–Rellich theorem establishes despite the Coulomb singularities (Appendix D.1.3). We assume that E1,…,EKE_{1},\ldots,E_{K} lie strictly below the essential spectrum of ℋ\mathpzc{H}, which begins at the first ionization limit (Appendix D.1.4). Since ℋ\mathpzc{H} has real coefficients in position space, its eigenstates can be chosen real-valued, and we restrict every ansatz to a real-valued function.11 1 This relies on the absence of external magnetic fields and of relativistic effects such as spin-orbit coupling, both outside the present scope.

2.1 Variational Monte Carlo for ground state computation

VMC minimizes the Rayleigh quotient of a wavefunction ansatz ψθ\psi_{\theta} with parameters θ\theta,

minθℒ(θ),ℒ(θ):=⟨ψθ​ℋ​ψθ⟩⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩=𝔼pθ​(𝐱)[ℰθ(𝐱)],\displaystyle\min_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta),\quad\mathcal{L}(\theta)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\bigl[\mathcal{E}_{\theta}({\bf x})\bigr],

where ℰθ(𝐱):=ℋ​ψθ​(𝐱)ψθ​(𝐱)\mathcal{E}_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}{\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})} is called the local energy, and pθ(𝐱):=ψθ​(𝐱)2⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩p_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle} is the induced probability density from the wavefunction ansatz, called the Born density. Then the gradient of the Rayleigh quotient is

∇θℒ​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta) =2​𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[Re((ℰθ​(𝐱)−𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[ℰθ​(𝐱)])​∇θ​log⁡ψθ∗​(𝐱))].\displaystyle=2\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\Bigl[\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\Bigl((\mathcal{E}_{\theta}({\bf x})-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}[\mathcal{E}_{\theta}({\bf x})])\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})\Bigr)\Bigr]. (1)

See Lemma E.1 for its proof. The gradient (1) can be estimated unbiasedly from walkers, samples drawn from the Born density pθp_{\theta} by a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm [4]. Since integrals over ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}} are otherwise intractable, VMC needs an objective, or at least its gradient, written as expectations under the Born densities of the ansatzes; we call such an objective or gradient VMC-compatible.

2.2 Prior works on excited states computation

Two VMC-compatible approaches exist: penalty-based methods tune penalty weights against the energy gaps, and NES-VMC needs K2K^{2} Laplacians per step.

(1) Penalty-Based Methods. Penalty-based methods [3, 23, 39, 37] keep the per-state Rayleigh quotient and add an explicit pairwise overlap penalty to enforce orthogonality:

ℒ𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒(ψ1:K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{penalty}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) =∑k=1K𝔼pk[ℰk]+∑k<ℓαk​ℓΠ(𝖲~k​ℓ),𝖲~k​ℓ:=⟨ψk​ψℓ⟩‖ψk‖​‖ψℓ‖,\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\mathcal{E}_{k}]+\sum_{k<\ell}\alpha_{k\ell}\,\Pi(\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{k\ell}),\quad\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{k\ell}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\ell}\rangle}{\|\psi_{k}\|\|\psi_{\ell}\|},

where ℰk(𝐱):=ℋ​ψ𝓀​(𝐱)ψk​(𝐱)\mathcal{E}_{k}({\bf x})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k}({\bf x})}{\psi_{k}({\bf x})} denotes the local energy of the kk-th ansatz and pk​(𝐱)∝ψk​(𝐱)2p_{k}({\bf x})\propto\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2} the corresponding Born density, αk​ℓ>0\alpha_{k\ell}>0 are penalty weights, and Π\Pi is a penalty kernel, such as Π⁡(s)=s2\Pi(s)=\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}s\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}, which admits an unbiased estimator [23, 39]. Wheeler et al. [39] established an ensemble variational principle showing that an energy-weighted version of this objective recovers the ordered lowest KK eigenfunctions of ℋ\mathpzc{H} once the overlap penalty exceeds a spectral-gap-dependent threshold (Appendix C.2). This threshold depends on the energy gaps, so the tuning depends on the very spectrum the optimization aims to compute. Based on this criterion, Szabó et al. [37] set each αk​ℓ\alpha_{k\ell} at every step to a global scale α~\tilde{\alpha} times the larger of two exponential moving averages (EMAs) over training steps: that of the energy gap between states kk and ℓ\ell and that of the local-energy standard deviation of state kk (Appendix C.2). Whether the global minimum gives the lowest KK eigenstates thus depends on how accurate these estimates are.

(2) NES-VMC. Pfau et al. [27] propose an extended-system construction for the lowest KK states. NES-VMC evaluates the KK ansatzes ψ1,…,ψK\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{K} on KK electron configurations 𝐗=(𝐱1,…,𝐱K){\bf X}=({\bf x}^{1},\ldots,{\bf x}^{K}) and forms the matrix ansatz Ψ⁡(𝐗)∈ℂK×K\Psi({\bf X})\in\mathbb{C}^{K\times K} with Ψi​k​(𝐗)=ψk​(𝐱i)\Psi_{ik}({\bf X})=\psi_{k}({\bf x}^{i}). The total ansatz is the determinant Φ(𝐗):=detΨ(𝐗)\Phi({\bf X})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\det\Psi({\bf X}). NES-VMC minimizes the energy of this extended system, in which ℋ\mathpzc{H} acts on each of the KK configurations 𝐱i{\bf x}^{i} and the results are summed. This energy has two forms (Theorems C.1 and C.2 in Appendix C.1)

ℒ𝖭𝖤𝖲​-​𝖵𝖬𝖢(ψ1:K)=tr(𝖲−1𝖧)=𝔼𝐗∼Φ2[tr(𝖤𝗅𝗈𝖼(𝐗))],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{NES\text{-}VMC}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})=\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\mathsf{S}^{-1}\mathsf{H})=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}\sim\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\Phi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}}\bigl[\mathop{\rm tr}\nolimits(\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{loc}}({\bf X}))\bigr], (2)

where 𝖲:=[⟨ψkψℓ⟩]k,ℓ=1K\mathsf{S}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=[\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\ell}\rangle]_{k,\ell=1}^{K} and 𝖧:=[⟨ψkℋψℓ⟩]𝓀,ℓ=1𝒦\mathsf{H}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=[\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\ell}\rangle]_{k,\ell=1}^{K} are the overlap and energy matrices, and 𝖤𝗅𝗈𝖼(𝐗):=Ψ(𝐗)−1(ℋΨ)(𝐗)\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{loc}}({\bf X})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\Psi({\bf X})^{-1}(\mathpzc{H}\Psi)({\bf X}) is the total local energy matrix with (ℋΨ)(𝐗):=[(ℋψ𝓀)(𝐱𝒾)]𝒾,𝓀=1𝒦(\mathpzc{H}\Psi)({\bf X})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=[\,(\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k})({\bf x}^{i})\,]_{i,k=1}^{K}. The matrix 𝖲−1​𝖧\mathsf{S}^{-1}\mathsf{H} represents ℋ\mathpzc{H} projected onto span{ψ1:K}\mathrm{span}\{\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}\}, so the middle form is the sum of the eigenvalues of this projected operator, minimized with value E1+⋯+EKE_{1}+\cdots+E_{K} by any KK ansatzes whose span is that of φ1,…,φK\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{K}. The right form of Eq. (2) is the ground-state VMC form on the KK-fold configuration space under the Born density Φ2/⟨Φ​Φ⟩\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\Phi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}/\langle\Phi~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\Phi\rangle of the total ansatz, written 𝐗∼Φ2{\bf X}\sim\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\Phi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}. The objective and its gradient are thus expectations under this density, so the objective is VMC-compatible. Since the minimum does not single out eigenfunctions within this span, NES-VMC orders and orthogonalizes the states in a post-processing step. This step diagonalizes the sample mean of 𝖤𝗅𝗈𝖼\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{loc}}, an estimate of 𝖲−1​𝖧\mathsf{S}^{-1}\mathsf{H} (Proposition C.1), and reads the individual energies from the eigenvalues of this mean. With this procedure, NES-VMC recovers accurate vertical excitation energies, including double excitations, on molecules up to the size of benzene.

NES-VMC incurs three structural costs, all from the total ansatz Φ=detΨ\Phi=\det\Psi through which it estimates (2). First, 𝖤𝗅𝗈𝖼\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{loc}} contains a cross term (ℋ​ψ𝓀)​(𝐱𝒾)(\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k})({\bf x}^{i}) for every pair (i,k)(i,k), and these K2K^{2} Laplacians per step dominate the wall time (Table 1). Second, the Born density of Φ\Phi couples all KK states in a single Markov chain, whereas penalty-based methods and NestedLoRA-VMC sample each state in its own chain, in parallel. Lastly, the gradient flows through the matrix inverse Ψ​(𝐗)−1\Psi({\bf X})^{-1}, which can become ill-conditioned when two ansatzes are nearly linearly dependent. We elaborate each point in Appendix I.2 and survey the numerical-stability measures of Pfau et al. [27] in Appendix H.6. Appendix B presents more related work on excited states and on learning eigenfunctions with neural networks.

3 Proposed method: NestedLoRA-VMC

This section adapts the NestedLoRA framework, developed for general operator decomposition, to excited-state VMC. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, is penalty-free and needs KK Laplacians per step. It inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle and learns the ordered eigenfunctions without explicit diagonalization. Sections 3.1 and 3.2 build the objective of NestedLoRA-VMC and its guarantee, and Sections 3.3 and 3.4 estimate it by Monte Carlo and compare its per-step cost with the two existing approaches.

3.1 Operator spectral decomposition via low-rank approximation

For a self-adjoint operator 𝒯\mathpzc{T} that is bounded above, suppose that we wish to recover its top-KK eigenvalues μ1≥μ2≥…≥μK\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\mu_{K} and corresponding orthonormal eigenfunctions φ1⟩,…,φK⟩\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\varphi_{1}\rangle,\ldots,\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\varphi_{K}\rangle. In our case, we will set 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H} such that μk=−Ek\mu_{k}=-E_{k}. Recently, Ryu et al. [30] proposed the low-rank approximation (LoRA) objective

ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(f1:K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) :=−2∑k=1K⟨fk𝒯𝒻𝓀⟩+∑k=1K∑ℓ=1K⟨fkfℓ⟩⟨fℓfk⟩,\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=-2\sum_{k=1}^{K}{\langle f_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}f_{k}\rangle}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}{\langle f_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~f_{\ell}\rangle\langle f_{\ell}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~f_{k}\rangle}, (3)

as a training objective for parametric spectral decomposition. For a Hilbert–Schmidt operator 𝒯\mathpzc{T}, this objective is equivalent to the rank-KK approximation error in Hilbert–Schmidt norm ∥𝒯−∑𝓀=1𝒦𝒻𝓀⟩⟨𝒻𝓀∥𝖧𝖲2\|\mathpzc{T}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\|_{\mathsf{HS}}^{2}. If this 𝒯\mathpzc{T} is moreover positive semidefinite and μK>μK+1\mu_{K}>\mu_{K+1}, a global minimizer f1:K⋆f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}^{\star} of ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(f1:K)\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) recovers the top-KK eigenspace of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} as ∑k=1Kfk⋆⟩⟨fk⋆=∑k=1Kμkφk⟩⟨φk\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}^{\star}\rangle\langle f_{k}^{\star}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\varphi_{k}\rangle\langle\varphi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}; for a self-adjoint 𝒯\mathpzc{T} with an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions, not necessarily compact or positive semidefinite, the minimizer recovers the top-min⁡(K,r)\min(K,r) eigenspace, where rr is the number of positive eigenvalues [30, Theorems 3.1 and C.5].

While neither result covers our quantum chemistry case 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H}, which is unbounded and has a continuous spectrum of scattering states, we show that the LoRA principle is still applicable when the lowest KK energies are eigenvalues below its essential spectrum (Appendix D.1.4). That is, a global minimizer recovers the top-KK eigenspace as above whenever μK>max⁡(μK+1,supσess​(𝒯),0)\mu_{K}>\max(\mu_{K+1},\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}),0), with σess​(𝒯)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}) the essential spectrum; the proof applies the Eckart–Young theorem to 𝒯\mathpzc{T} projected onto the span of f1:Kf_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}, the only part of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} on which the LoRA objective depends (Appendix D).

3.2 NestedLoRA-VMC

The LoRA objective requires a reparameterization to be VMC-compatible. Ryu et al. [30] further propose an optimization technique called nesting to learn ordered eigenfunctions without explicit diagonalization, and call the framework NestedLoRA.

Reparameterization.

The key idea for VMC-compatibility is to reparameterize each function fkf_{k} in (3) as λk​ψk/‖ψk‖\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}\,\psi_{k}/\|\psi_{k}\|, with the ansatzes ψ1:K\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} parameterized as neural networks with parameters θ\theta and λ1:K∈ℝ≥0K\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{K} as additional trainable scale parameters. Under the sequential nesting introduced below, each λk\lambda_{k} plays the role of the kk-th eigenvalue estimate. This yields the objective

𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:K,λ1:K):=−2∑k=1Kλk𝖱k​k𝒯+∑k,ℓ=1Kλkλℓ𝖱k​ℓℐ𝖱ℓ​kℐ,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=-2\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\mathsf{R}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}+\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\lambda_{\ell}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}},

where we define the generic functional 𝖱k​ℓ𝒪:=⟨ψk​𝒪​ψℓ⟩⟨ψk​ψk⟩=𝔼pk[𝒪​ψℓψk]\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\frac{\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}}{\psi_{k}}] for a symmetric operator 𝒪∈{𝒯,ℐ}\mathpzc{O}\in\{\mathpzc{T},\mathpzc{I}\}. The objective is VMC-compatible: drawing electronic configurations 𝐗{\bf X} from the product distribution ψ1(𝐱1)2⋯ψK(𝐱K)2\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{1}({\bf x}^{1})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}\cdots\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{K}({\bf x}^{K})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2} yields unbiased estimates of the objective and its gradient ∇θ𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}} (Theorem E.1).

Sequential nesting for learning ordered excited states.

As in Ryu et al. [31], we order the learned eigenfunctions by sequential nesting. Sequential nesting updates each network kk by the gradient with respect to ψk\psi_{k} of the order-kk objective 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k}), the LoRA objective of the first kk states, and updates all KK networks at once. This update can be read as KK nested problems solved together: if states 1,…,k−11,\ldots,k-1 are the first k−1k-1 eigenpairs, the order-kk objective is minimized by ψk∝φk\psi_{k}\propto\varphi_{k} and λk=μk\lambda_{k}=\mu_{k}, so the fixed point of the update is the ordered eigenpairs (Appendix D.4).

We define the sequential nesting gradient as

∇θ𝗌𝖾𝗊\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}^{\mathsf{seq}} :=14∑k=1K⟨∇θψk∂ψk𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)⟩=∑k=1KλkRe{−Δ~k​k𝒯+∑ℓ=1K𝖬k​ℓ𝗌𝖾𝗊λℓ𝖱ℓ​kℐΔ~k​ℓℐ},\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\langle\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathop{}\!\partial_{\psi_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k})\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\Bigl\{-\tilde{\Delta}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\mathsf{M}_{k\ell}^{\mathsf{seq}}\lambda_{\ell}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\Bigr\}, (4)

where ∂ψk\mathop{}\!\partial_{\psi_{k}} is the functional derivative with respect to ψk\psi_{k}, 𝖬k​ℓ𝗌𝖾𝗊=𝟙{k>ℓ}\mathsf{M}_{k\ell}^{\mathsf{seq}}=\mathds{1}\{k>\ell\} is the strictly lower-triangular mask and Δ~k​ℓ𝒪:=Covpk(𝒪ψℓ/ψ𝓀,∇θlogψ𝓀∗)\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathop{\rm Cov}\nolimits_{p_{k}}(\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k},\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{k}^{*}) is the covariance, under pkp_{k}, of the operator action 𝒪​ψℓ/ψ𝓀\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k} against the per-state score ∇θ​log​ψk∗\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{k}^{*} (using score in the same log-derivative sense as in eq. (1)), for 𝒪∈{𝒯,ℐ}\mathpzc{O}\in\{\mathpzc{T},\mathpzc{I}\}. Appendices E.1.2 and E.1.4 derive Eq. (4). For real-valued ansatzes the gradient is VMC-compatible, a sum over states of expectations under the Born densities pkp_{k}, estimated by averages over samples 𝐱∼pk{\bf x}\sim p_{k}, for each k∈[K]k\in[K]:

∇θ𝗌𝖾𝗊\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}^{\mathsf{seq}} =∑k=1K𝔼pk​(𝐱)​[(gk​(𝐱)−𝔼pk​[gk])​∇θ​log⁡ψk],\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}({\bf x})}\!\Bigl[(g_{k}({\bf x})-\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[g_{k}])\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\Bigr],
gk​(𝐱)\displaystyle g_{k}({\bf x}) :=λk(−𝒯​ψ𝓀​(𝐱)ψk​(𝐱)+∑ℓ=1K𝖬k​ℓ𝗌𝖾𝗊λℓ𝖱ℓ​kℐψℓ​(𝐱)ψk​(𝐱)).\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\lambda_{k}\Bigg(-\,\frac{\mathpzc{T}\psi_{k}({\bf x})}{\psi_{k}({\bf x})}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\mathsf{M}_{k\ell}^{\mathsf{seq}}\,\lambda_{\ell}\,\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\,\frac{\psi_{\ell}({\bf x})}{\psi_{k}({\bf x})}\Bigg). (5)

In our implementation, we drop the prefactor λk\lambda_{k} in gk​(𝐱)g_{k}({\bf x}) to normalize the gradient norm, which can be equivalently understood as using the state-dependent learning rate η/λk\eta/\lambda_{k} for a base learning rate η\eta; this rescales the gradient of each state by a positive factor and keeps the fixed point. A similar state-dependent learning rate was recently studied for kk-SVD by gradient descent with the LoRA principle [13].

3.3 Implementation details

In Sections 3.1 and 3.2, we derive a parametric gradient for finding the ordered eigenpairs as a fixed point out of iterative gradient-based updates. In practical optimization, there exist several issues that hinder effective training with a direct implementation of the gradient above: heavy-tails of the local energy and overlap statistics, the step-size sensitivity of the gradient-based eigenvalue updates, the conditioning of each network’s objective, and unstable order of the states at the beginning of training. The first is a statistical issue, while the rest are related to optimization. In this section, we provide a solution to each problem without altering the fixed-point property of the desired solution.

3.3.1 Asymmetric clipping for local energy and overlap statistics

To implement the gradient in Eq. (5), we need the local energy statistics 𝒯​ψ𝓀/ψ𝓀\mathpzc{T}\psi_{k}/\psi_{k} and local overlap statistics ψℓ/ψk\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k}. Since both statistics may blow up around the nodes of ψk\psi_{k} (i.e., where ψk≈0\psi_{k}\approx 0), it is a common practice in the literature [26, 38, 27, 37] to apply a clipping on these values. However, we empirically find that an asymmetric clipping strategy, clipping local energies while using raw local overlap statistics, leads to much more stable training; we attribute the effectiveness of the asymmetric clipping rule to differences in how the statistics behave near convergence, as explained below.

First, note that the local energy 𝒯​ψ𝓀/ψ𝓀\mathpzc{T}\psi_{k}/\psi_{k} is constant at the fixed point, so the clipping is inactive there; Appendix F.1 gives the clipping rule. In contrast, the local overlap ψℓ/ψk\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k} stays heavy-tailed at the fixed point; theoretically, we can show that, under the Born density pkp_{k}, the probability that its magnitude exceeds tt decays as t−3t^{-3} under regularity conditions; see Appendix F.2.1. This suggests that, for example, the clipping rule of Szabó et al. [37], which clips outside the median ±10\pm 10 median absolute deviations, may still unexpectedly perturb some walkers even around convergence, since the heavy tail places some walkers outside the clip window; see Figure 4c in Appendix F.2.2. The perturbation can bias the batch mean of the ratio, whose expectation 𝖱k​ℓℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}_{k\ell} vanishes at the fixed point.

We demonstrate empirically on Li that clipping the ratio substantially biases its batch mean, both early in training and near convergence. Early in training, when the overlap remains nonzero and the overlap term helps separate the networks, clipping shifts the batch mean away from a reference estimate obtained using long Metropolis chains targeting a mixture of pkp_{k} and pℓp_{\ell}, by an amount many times larger than its variation across batches; see Figure 4. At the final training step, near a fixed point at which the overlap should vanish, the clip still changes the walkers of many ratios and can leave their batch means spuriously nonzero; see Appendix F.2.2.

3.3.2 Analytical eigenvalue updates

A gradient update of the eigenvalue parameters λ1:K\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} together with the networks needs a step size for λ\lambda, which may be hard to tune together with training the neural ansatzes. To simplify the updates, we instead propose to track the eigenvalues by an analytical update at each step. Since the objective 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k}) is strictly convex quadratic in λk\lambda_{k}, we solve its stationary equation ⁡∂λk𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠=0\mathop{}\!\partial_{\lambda_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}=0 to obtain an analytical update. Mirroring the sequential update of ψk\psi_{k}, we hold the lower-state parameters {λj:j<k}\{\lambda_{j}\colon j<k\} fixed and solve ⁡∂λk𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠=0\mathop{}\!\partial_{\lambda_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}=0 sequentially for k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, yielding

𝝀⋆\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star} =(𝖨+𝖬𝗌𝖾𝗊⊙(𝖱ℐ⊙(𝖱ℐ)⊺))−1​diag(𝖱𝒯),\displaystyle=\bigl(\mathsf{I}+\mathsf{M}^{\mathsf{seq}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}})^{\intercal})\bigr)^{-1}\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}), (6)

which can be computed in one cheap O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}) triangular sweep per step; Appendix E.2 gives the step-by-step derivation. Because the system is lower-triangular, a heavy-tailed estimate at state mm enters λj⋆\lambda^{\star}_{j} only for j≥mj\geq m. In practice, we plug EMAs of the estimates of 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} and diag(𝖱𝒯)\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}) into Eq. (6) to smooth the trajectory across steps. With the exact 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} and diag(𝖱𝒯)\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}) in place of these estimates, the solve returns λk=μk\lambda_{k}=\mu_{k} at the ordered eigenpairs, so the fixed point is unchanged.

3.3.3 Per-network operator shifts for curvature shaping

Another source of instability in the sequential nesting gradient of Eq. (5) is the imbalance between its energy and overlap terms. While the energy term distinguishes eigenstates through spectral gaps, the overlap term is weighted by λℓ≈−Eℓ\lambda_{\ell}\approx-E_{\ell}, whose magnitude can be much larger than the spectral gaps. This creates steep directions toward lower eigenstates and relatively flat directions toward higher ones, leading to unstable convergence.

To mitigate this imbalance, we introduce a network-specific operator shift. Since network kk is updated only through the kk-th term of Eq. (4), it can use 𝒯𝓀:=ℰref,𝓀ℐ−ℋ\mathpzc{T}_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=E_{\mathrm{ref},k}\mathpzc{I}-\mathpzc{H}, with Eref,kE_{\mathrm{ref},k} fixed during gradient computation. The shift adds a constant −Eref,k-E_{\mathrm{ref},k} to the local energy, which vanishes upon centering, while changing each lower-state overlap coefficient from λℓ≈−Eℓ\lambda_{\ell}\approx-E_{\ell} to λℓ+Eref,k≈Eref,k−Eℓ\lambda_{\ell}+E_{\mathrm{ref},k}\approx E_{\mathrm{ref},k}-E_{\ell} near orthogonality. Thus, choosing Eref,kE_{\mathrm{ref},k} near EkE_{k} reduces the relative weight of the overlap term without changing the centered energy contribution.

To see its effect on curvature, assume ψℓ∝φℓ\psi_{\ell}\propto\varphi_{\ell} for ℓ<k\ell<k and expand qk:=ψk‖ψk‖=∑nak​nφn+χkq_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\psi_{k}}{\|\psi_{k}\|}=\sum_{n}a_{kn}\varphi_{n}+\chi_{k}, where φn\varphi_{n} are the discrete eigenfunctions of ℋ\mathpzc{H} with energies EnE_{n}, and χk\chi_{k} belongs to its essential spectral subspace. The effective objective underlying the kk-th gradient, with the prefactor λk\lambda_{k} removed, is approximately Ek+∑ℓ<k(Eref,k−Ek)​ak​ℓ2+∑n>k(En−Ek)​ak​n2+⟨χk​(ℋ−ℰ𝓀)​χ𝓀⟩E_{k}+\sum_{\ell<k}(E_{\mathrm{ref},k}-E_{k})\,a_{k\ell}^{2}+\sum_{n>k}(E_{n}-E_{k})\,a_{kn}^{2}+\langle\chi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~(\mathpzc{H}-E_{k})\chi_{k}\rangle. Thus, the lower-state curvature decreases from −Ek-E_{k} to Eref,k−EkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}-E_{k}, while the higher-state curvature remains unchanged.

In our implementation, we choose Eref,k=−λk+c​σkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}=-\lambda_{k}+c\,\sigma_{k}, where −λk-\lambda_{k} estimates EkE_{k} via Eq. (6), σk\sigma_{k} is the walker standard deviation of the clipped local energy, and c=5c=5. The margin c​σkc\,\sigma_{k} helps ensure Eref,k>EkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}>E_{k}, so that the target state retains a positive eigenvalue under 𝒯𝓀\mathpzc{T}_{k} and remains recoverable by LoRA. Near convergence, the lower-state curvature becomes approximately c​σkc\,\sigma_{k} rather than Ek\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}E_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}. Whenever Eref,k>EkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}>E_{k}, φk\varphi_{k} remains a minimizer, up to degeneracies. Appendix G.1 analyzes the curvature imbalance for carbon, and Section 4.4 demonstrates the effect of the shift.

3.3.4 Online state ordering for faster convergence

We find that online state reordering lets the networks learn the lowest KK states without waiting for their energies to line up with their indices during training. We assign, at every step, the order-kk objective to the network whose EMA energy ranks kk-th within its spin sector (Section 4.1 and Appendix G.2). The ranking reads only the EMA energies, so it is the same under every shift Eref,kE_{\mathrm{ref},k} of Section 3.3.3. The assignment changes only which network carries which index, so the fixed point is unchanged.

3.4 Choice of parameterization and per-iteration efficiency

NestedLoRA-VMC needs KK Laplacians per step, against K2K^{2} for NES-VMC. Like the penalty methods, NestedLoRA-VMC applies ℋ\mathpzc{H} to each state only at that state’s own walkers, (ℋ​ψ𝓀)​(𝐱𝓀)(\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k})({\bf x}^{k}), while the local-energy matrix of NES-VMC needs (ℋ​ψ𝓀)​(𝐱𝒾)(\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k})({\bf x}^{i}) at every pair (i,k)(i,k). A Laplacian is the most expensive evaluation in a step: it sums 3​n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}} second derivatives, so with the forward Laplacian [19] it costs about 3​n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}} forward evaluations, O⁡(n𝖾𝗅4)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{4}) against O⁡(n𝖾𝗅3)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{3}) for one forward evaluation (Appendix I.1).

FermiNet [26] and the Psiformer [38] compute a feature of each electron with a backbone of permutation-equivariant layers, map these features to an orbital matrix, and sum the determinants of such matrices. Within one forward evaluation, the determinant of the orbital matrix sets the order n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{3}, and on first-row atoms most of the cost is in the dense layers of the backbone, which act on a 256256-dimensional feature of each electron. These costs, times the number of forward evaluations per step that Appendix I.2 counts by component, give the theoretical scaling in Table 1. The per-step wall time measured on Ne follows it for NES-VMC, the penalty class [37, Figure 1] and NestedLoRA-VMC (Appendix I.3).

NES-VMC uses one joint backbone with KK heads, each of which maps the shared features of the electrons to the orbital matrices of one state. Whether this costs less than KK disjoint networks depends on where ℋ\mathpzc{H} is applied. In NES-VMC every state needs its Laplacian at every walker set, and a joint backbone computes the backbone’s part once per walker set for all KK heads. In NestedLoRA-VMC and the penalty methods each state needs its Laplacian only at its own walkers, so the Laplacian costs the same under either parameterization, and a joint backbone saves only on the overlaps, which carry no factor 3​n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}. We use KK disjoint networks, following Szabó et al. [37].

4 Experiments

We evaluate NestedLoRA-VMC on the first-row atoms, Li through Ne, with the Psiformer architecture [38], for the lowest K=10K{=}10 eigenstates of ℋ\mathpzc{H}. Its excited-state energies are comparable in accuracy to those of NES-VMC [27] and the penalty-based method of Szabó et al. [37], against term centroids from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) (Section 4.2). On carbon, the per-network operator-shift of Section 3.3.3 brings the five networks of the degenerate 2​p2​D12p^{2}\,{}^{1}\!D level close together in energy, whereas with 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H} they stay spread over the level (Section 4.4).22 2 Source code for NestedLoRA-VMC is available at https://github.com/MinchanJeong/NestedLoRA-VMC.

4.1 Setup

Ansatz and MCMC sampler.

Every network is a Psiformer [38] and samples its own Born density with one Metropolis chain; Appendix H.2 gives the sampler settings.

Pretraining.

For every atom we pretrain to a complete-active-space self-consistent-field (CASSCF) target with aug-cc-pVTZ as the underlying single-particle basis. The active space (Ne,No)(N_{e},N_{o}), NeN_{e} electrons in NoN_{o} orbitals, is chosen per atom to cover the K=10K{=}10 states of its sectors (Table 6). The per-state CASSCF targets and the pretraining schedule are in Appendix H.5.

Spin sectors and spin penalty.

To obtain pure spin states more accurately, we run NestedLoRA-VMC on 𝒯=−(ℋ+𝒮^2)\mathpzc{T}=-(\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2}) so that each state has one total spin SS. The numbers n↑n_{\uparrow} and n↓n_{\downarrow} of Section 2 fix mS=(n↑−n↓)/2m_{S}=(n_{\uparrow}-n_{\downarrow})/2, so the spin sector of a given mSm_{S} holds every state with S≥mSS\geq\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} (cf. Pfau et al. [26], von Glehn et al. [38]). Added to ℋ\mathpzc{H}, the spin penalty S^2\hat{S}^{2} raises each state by S⁡(S+1)S(S{+}1) and keeps the eigenfunctions, so the lowest states of a sector take its smallest spin S=mSS=\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} (Appendix D.3.3). In training, each atom has one sector mS=Sm_{S}=S for each spin multiplicity 2​S+12S{+}1 among its lowest K=10K{=}10 states; the sectors, with fixed numbers of networks that sum to K=10K{=}10, are trained in one run, and their states are merged by energy. Szabó et al. [37] use this penalty for every atom and fix mSm_{S} for each higher spin multiplicity, which gives the same sectors (Appendix H.4).

Reference data.

A term L2​S+1{}^{2S+1}\!L has total spin SS and total orbital angular momentum LL, with L=0,1,2L=0,1,2 written S, P, D; Table 6 gives the terms of each atom. We compare energies with term centroids from the NIST atomic-spectroscopy compilation of Sansonetti and Martin [32]. The centroid of a term is the mean energy of its fine-structure levels J=L−S,…,L+SJ=\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}L-S\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{},\ldots,L+S, each weighted by its degeneracy 2​J+12J{+}1; spin–orbit coupling splits a term into these levels, and ℋ\mathpzc{H} gives them one energy. NIST gives each level as its energy above the ground level, so every comparison uses the excitation energy Δ​E\Delta E of each state above the ground-term centroid.

Training.

Training runs are 100,000100{,}000 steps at an electron batch of 4,0964{,}096 with the Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (KFAC) optimizer [21], a natural-gradient approximation applied per state (Appendix H.3).

4.2 Excited-state energies on first-row atoms

The per-atom mean absolute error (MAE) of NestedLoRA-VMC in Table 2 is below chemical accuracy on every atom from Li to F and comparable to that of NES-VMC [27] and of the penalty-based method of Szabó et al. [37]. NES-VMC reaches its MAE with 200,000200{,}000 training steps per atom [27, Table S1], twice the 100,000100{,}000 of NestedLoRA-VMC and of Szabó et al. [37, SI Table S6].

Figure 1 shows the recovered K=10K{=}10 spectra on each atom. All three methods are scored against the same NIST term centroids, with the NES-VMC and penalty errors computed from the per-state values published in their papers. Per-state energies of NestedLoRA-VMC are the mean of the per-walker local energy over the last 3,0003{,}000 training steps, evaluated with exact interparticle distances (Appendix J). The compute time available set the number of training seeds per atom: three for Li, Be and B, two for C and Ne, and one for N, O and F. Appendix J gives the scoring, the per-state errors of all eight atoms, and in Table 8 the 95%95\% interval of each run’s MAE.

4.3 Overlap of the trained networks

Exact eigenstates are mutually orthogonal, so we measure the normalized overlap of every pair of networks within a spin sector at the final training step as a surrogate for how well the networks learn the eigenstates, with the long chains of Appendix F.2.2 (Figure 2). The trained networks are close to orthogonal on every atom from Li to F.

4.4 On the effectiveness of the per-network operator-shift on carbon

On carbon we test whether the shift of Section 3.3.3 improves the energy convergence of the five networks of the 2​p22p^{2} D1{}^{1}\!D term, whose exact energies are equal. We train 5,0005{,}000 steps from the pretrained start of the seed-11 carbon run of Table 2, with the setup of Section 4.1 and training seeds 11 and 22. For each seed one run uses Eref,k=0E_{\mathrm{ref},k}=0, that is 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H}, and one the shift Eref,k=−λk+5​σkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}=-\lambda_{k}+5\sigma_{k} (Figure 3). With Eref,k=0E_{\mathrm{ref},k}=0 the five networks stay spread over the term. With the shift their mean energies over the last 1,0001{,}000 steps span less than a tenth as much.

5 Conclusion

We present NestedLoRA-VMC, a new approach to excited-state VMC based on nested low-rank approximation. Unlike penalty-based methods and NES-VMC, NestedLoRA-VMC exploits the structure of the spectral approximation problem to recover eigenstates in energy order while retaining per-network VMC optimization. This provides a principled alternative to existing approaches, with computational savings in Laplacian evaluations that become increasingly significant as the number of target states grows.

An important next step is to extend NestedLoRA-VMC to molecular systems and larger KK. Its VMC-compatible formulation also opens opportunities to incorporate advanced optimization techniques, such as Wasserstein gradient flows [22] and improved discretizations of imaginary-time evolution [36].

Limitations.

Empirical validation is limited to first-row atoms (Li–Ne) at K=10K{=}10. For molecular systems, reference excitation energies at fixed nuclear geometries are best estimates whose uncertainty grows with system size, motivating evaluation criteria beyond agreement with reference values. Our multi-spin calculations also require preselecting spin sectors and allocating networks among them; automating this selection remains an open problem. Finally, NestedLoRA-VMC retains the O⁡(n𝖾𝗅4)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{4}) Laplacian cost of standard neural-network VMC, which remains a major bottleneck for larger molecules. Reducing this cost requires further mathematical and computational advances.

Appendix B Related work

NestedLoRA-VMC is penalty-free like NES-VMC and needs KK Laplacians per step like the penalty-based methods. It takes its objective from the neural-network eigensolver NestedLoRA and learns the states in energy order through sequential nesting (Section 3.2).

Ab initio methods for excited states.

The accurate methods of ab initio quantum chemistry grow steeply in cost with the number n𝖾𝗅{n_{\mathsf{el}}} of electrons. Full configuration interaction expands ψ\psi in Slater determinants and gives the ordered eigenstates exactly, but needs exponentially many determinants [26]. Coupled cluster with single, double and perturbative triple excitations, CCSD(T), costs O⁡(n𝖾𝗅7)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{7}) for the ground state [38], and equation-of-motion coupled cluster costs O⁡(n𝖾𝗅6)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{6}) or more for excited states [35, 18]. Time-dependent density functional theory is far cheaper, but its usual approximations fail for long-range charge-transfer excitations and miss double excitations [2, 20].

Neural-network VMC for the ground state.

Neural-network VMC represents the wavefunction by a neural network and minimizes its energy with stochastic optimizers [17, 21], using samples of the Born density as in Section 2; Hermann et al. [11] review the field. On the ground states of small molecules, FermiNet [26], PauliNet [10] and Psiformer [38] reach chemical accuracy, an error below 11 kcal/mol or about 1.61.6 millihartree (mHa). With the forward Laplacian [19], each optimization step costs O⁡(n𝖾𝗅4)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{4}) for a fixed network size, against O⁡(n𝖾𝗅7)O({n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{7}) for CCSD(T). NestedLoRA-VMC keeps this machinery for every state: each ψk\psi_{k} is its own network and is sampled from its own Born density.

Excited-state VMC.

Penalty-based methods [23, 3, 39, 37] train one ansatz per state on the sum of the energies plus pairwise overlap penalties, and the penalty weights set whether the minimum is the ordered eigenstates. Gao et al. [6] train one network for many excited states across molecular geometries on a penalty objective, and estimate the overlaps from samples pooled over all states.

NES-VMC [27] minimizes the energy of an extended system whose ansatz is the determinant of the KK ansatzes evaluated on KK configurations, and obtains the individual states by a diagonalization after training. The inverse of this K×KK\times K matrix enters its local energy, which therefore develops heavy tails when two ansatzes are nearly linearly dependent. Hendry et al. [8] write this objective as the energy of a KK-dimensional subspace and derive a stochastic reconfiguration on the manifold of such subspaces, and Kahn et al. [15] derive the same formalism and apply it to time evolution. Section 2.2 describes the penalty-based methods and NES-VMC, and Appendix C states their objectives in full.

Neural-network eigensolvers.

Outside VMC, several methods learn the leading eigenfunctions of an operator with neural networks and estimate inner products under a fixed data or proposal distribution. SpIN [25] maximizes a trace objective whitened by the covariance of the learned functions and orders them with a masked gradient. NeuralEF [1] solves a sequence of Rayleigh-quotient problems in which each function is penalized against the earlier ones. NestedLoRA [30] minimizes the error of a rank-KK approximation of the operator, a polynomial in the inner products of the learned functions, and orders the eigenfunctions by nesting, which descends from the triangularized gradient of Gao et al. [7].

NestedLoRA-VMC brings the NestedLoRA objective to VMC: the reparameterization of Section 3.2 writes it as expectations under the Born densities of the ansatzes. NestedLoRA has been applied to low-dimensional partial differential equations and representation learning [30] and to the Koopman operators of stochastic dynamical systems [14]; Ryu et al. [31] apply nesting to the objective of the orbital minimization method, and Jedra and Shah [13] study kk-SVD by gradient descent with the same low-rank-approximation principle.

C.2 Penalty-based methods

PauliNet penalty (Entwistle et al., 2023).

Entwistle et al. [3] extended PauliNet to excited states with the divergent overlap penalty

ℒ𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒(ψ1:K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{penalty}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) =∑k=1K𝔼pk[ℰk]+α∑i<j11−𝖲~i​j,𝖲~i​j:=⟨ψi​ψj⟩‖ψi‖​‖ψj‖.\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\mathcal{E}_{k}]+\alpha\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{1-\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{ij}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}},\quad\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{ij}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\langle\psi_{i}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{j}\rangle}{\|\psi_{i}\|\|\psi_{j}\|}.

The symmetrized overlap is estimated consistently by the product of expectations

𝖲~i​j\displaystyle\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{ij} =sgn(𝔼pi​[ψjψi])×𝔼pi​[ψjψi]​𝔼pj​[ψiψj].\displaystyle=\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits\biggl(\mathbb{E}_{p_{i}}\biggl[\frac{\psi_{j}}{\psi_{i}}\biggr]\biggr)\times\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{p_{i}}\biggl[\frac{\psi_{j}}{\psi_{i}}\biggr]\mathbb{E}_{p_{j}}\biggl[\frac{\psi_{i}}{\psi_{j}}\biggr]}.
Pathak–Wheeler form.

Pathak et al. [23], Wheeler et al. [39] use a squared overlap that admits a direct unbiased estimator,

ℒ𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗍𝗒(ψ1:K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{penalty}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) =∑k=1K𝔼pk​[ℰk]+∑i<jαi​j​𝖲~i​j2.\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\mathcal{E}_{k}]+\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{ij}\,\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{ij}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}.

Wheeler et al. [39] established an ensemble variational principle for this family. Its objective carries strictly decreasing energy weights w1>⋯>wK>0w_{1}>\cdots>w_{K}>0 on ∑iwi​𝔼pi​[ℰi]\sum_{i}w_{i}\mathbb{E}_{p_{i}}[\mathcal{E}_{i}] and a single global penalty α​∑i<j𝖲~i​j2\alpha\sum_{i<j}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{ij}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}. The ordered bottom-KK eigenfunctions of ℋ\mathpzc{H} are then the global minimum once α>αc=maxi<j⁡[(Ej−Ei)​wi​wj/(wi−wj)]\alpha>\alpha_{c}=\max_{i<j}\bigl[(E_{j}-E_{i})\,w_{i}w_{j}/(w_{i}-w_{j})\bigr], with EiE_{i} the eigenvalues the optimum identifies. The strictly decreasing weights break the rotational degeneracy of the bottom-KK subspace: at equal weights αc→∞\alpha_{c}\to\infty and the minimum is the subspace, not its ordered basis. Because αc\alpha_{c} scales with the spectral gaps Ej−EiE_{j}-E_{i}, the penalty schedule is coupled to the spectrum the optimization computes. The per-pair αi​j\alpha_{ij} form displayed above is the practical variant; Szabó et al. [37] scale αi​j\alpha_{ij} to running gap estimates (below).

Szabó et al. [37] adopted the Pathak–Wheeler form with three modifications. First, the orthogonality constraint is applied with respect to lower-lying states only: gradients of the overlap term flow only into ψj\psi_{j} for j>ij>i, while ψi\psi_{i} is detached from the computational graph (their Section 2.1.2). Second, an explicit per-state spin penalty β​∑i⟨S^2⟩i\beta\sum_{i}\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle_{i} (their Eq. 7) selects the target spin sector at training time; Appendix G.3 gives the corresponding operator shift in our framework, and Appendix H.4 the spin sectors that their setting implies. Third, αi​j\alpha_{ij} is set at every step to (their Eq. 17)

αi​j=α~⋅max{ema(E^j−E^i),ema(stdpi(ℰi)), 0.001} 1{i<j},\displaystyle\alpha_{ij}=\tilde{\alpha}\cdot\max\bigl\{\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\mathrm{ema}(\hat{E}_{j}-\hat{E}_{i})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{},\ \mathrm{ema}(\mathrm{std}_{p_{i}}(\mathcal{E}_{i})),\ 0.001\bigr\}\,\mathds{1}\{i<j\},

where E^i\hat{E}_{i} is the batch mean of ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i}, stdpi​(ℰi)\mathrm{std}_{p_{i}}(\mathcal{E}_{i}) is its batch standard deviation, and ema⁡(⋅)\mathrm{ema}(\,\cdot\,) is an EMA over training steps. This reduces the user-tunable hyperparameter to a single global scale α~\tilde{\alpha} (default α~=4\tilde{\alpha}=4, with α~=2\tilde{\alpha}=2 for Li, Be and α~=1\tilde{\alpha}=1 for benzene per their SI Table S6).

Appendix D Discussion on the mathematical formulation

The LoRA objective of NestedLoRA-VMC is well defined for the molecular Hamiltonian, its global minimizers span the lowest KK eigenstates, and the fixed point of sequential nesting gives these eigenstates in energy order. The first claim holds for any KK trial functions in ℋ\mathscr{H}, because the objective of the unbounded 𝒯\mathpzc{T} is the Hilbert–Schmidt objective of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} projected onto their span, an operator of finite rank (Appendix D.2). The other two claims hold when the lowest KK energies of ℋ\mathpzc{H} lie strictly below its essential spectrum, which we assume in Appendix D.1.4, and are shown in Appendices D.3 and D.4.

D.1 Mathematical preliminaries

The three claims are statements about ℋ\mathpzc{H} on the spatial space ℋ\mathscr{H}, and this subsection gives the mathematical facts about ℋ\mathscr{H} and the spectrum of ℋ\mathpzc{H} that their proofs use.

D.1.1 Reduction to the spatial space ℋ\mathscr{H}

The eigenstates of the electrons with n↑n_{\uparrow} spins up correspond one-to-one to the eigenfunctions of ℋ\mathpzc{H} in ℋ\mathscr{H}, with the same energies, and their levels are those of total spin S≥mSS\geq\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}, where mS=(n↑−n↓)/2m_{S}=(n_{\uparrow}-n_{\downarrow})/2.

The space ℋ\mathscr{H} is the subspace of L2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}) of functions of the electron positions 𝐱=(𝐫1,…,𝐫n𝖾𝗅){\bf x}=(\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{n_{\mathsf{el}}}) that are antisymmetric under the exchange of two electrons of the same spin, where electrons 1,…,n↑1,\ldots,n_{\uparrow} have spin up and the other n↓=n𝖾𝗅−n↑n_{\downarrow}={n_{\mathsf{el}}}-n_{\uparrow} have spin down. The antisymmetrizer over the permutations within each spin is an orthogonal projection with range ℋ\mathscr{H}, so ℋ\mathscr{H} is closed and is a Hilbert space with the inner product of L2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}). Our network architecture restricts the functions it can represent to ℋ\mathscr{H} by construction (Appendix H.1).

An electronic state (state in this section) is a function of the positions and spins of the electrons, an element of L2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)⊗(ℂ2)⊗n𝖾𝗅L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}})\otimes(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes{n_{\mathsf{el}}}} that changes sign when two electrons exchange both position and spin. The states with n↑n_{\uparrow} spins up correspond one-to-one to the functions in ℋ\mathscr{H}, and the correspondence is a linear isomorphism: it maps ψ∈ℋ\psi\in\mathscr{H} to the antisymmetrization Ψ\Psi, over all electrons, of ψ\psi times the spin function with electrons 1,…,n↑1,\ldots,n_{\uparrow} up. Since ℋ\mathpzc{H} acts on the positions alone and is symmetric in the electrons, it acts on states as ℋ⊗ℐ\mathpzc{H}\otimes\mathpzc{I}, which commutes with this antisymmetrization, so (ℋ⊗ℐ)​Ψ=ℰ​Ψ(\mathpzc{H}\otimes\mathpzc{I})\Psi=E\Psi exactly when ℋ​ψ=ℰ​ψ\mathpzc{H}\psi=E\psi.

The total spin operators S^2\hat{S}^{2}, with eigenvalues S⁡(S+1)S(S{+}1), and S^z\hat{S}_{z} act on the spins of the states, and the states with n↑n_{\uparrow} spins up form the eigenspace of S^z\hat{S}_{z} with eigenvalue mSm_{S}. Both commute with ℋ⊗ℐ\mathpzc{H}\otimes\mathpzc{I}, so each of its eigenspaces is spanned by multiplets of total spin SS, each consisting of 2​S+12S+1 states with S^z\hat{S}_{z} eigenvalues −S,…,S-S,\ldots,S [24, Sections 5.2–5.3]. A multiplet contains one state with n↑n_{\uparrow} spins up exactly when S≥mSS\geq\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}, so the states with n↑n_{\uparrow} spins up form the orthogonal sum of their subspaces of total spin S=mS,mS+1,…,n𝖾𝗅/2S=\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{},\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}+1,\ldots,{n_{\mathsf{el}}}/2, each left invariant by ℋ⊗ℐ\mathpzc{H}\otimes\mathpzc{I}. Through the isomorphism, ℋ=⨁S≥mSℋ(S)\mathscr{H}=\bigoplus_{S\geq\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}}\mathscr{H}^{(S)}, where ℋ(S)\mathscr{H}^{(S)} corresponds to total spin SS and is left invariant by ℋ\mathpzc{H}, and the eigenvalues of ℋ\mathpzc{H} in ℋ\mathscr{H} are the energies of total spin S≥mSS\geq\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}, with one eigenfunction per multiplet.

Example: lithium.

The antisymmetry that defines ℋ\mathscr{H} excludes functions with energy below the physical ground state. Consider lithium with mSm_{S} fixed at 1/21/2, that is, n↑=2n_{\uparrow}=2 and n↓=1n_{\downarrow}=1. The spatial function 1​s​(𝐫1)​ 1​s​(𝐫2)​ 1​s​(𝐫3)1s(\mathbf{r}_{1})\,1s(\mathbf{r}_{2})\,1s(\mathbf{r}_{3}) of three hydrogenic orbitals is symmetric in the three electrons and, for a suitable orbital exponent, has an energy below the physical ground state; it lies outside ℋ\mathscr{H}, because it is symmetric under the exchange of the two spin-up electrons.

D.1.2 Self-adjoint operators and their spectrum

The min–max values of a self-adjoint operator 𝒯\mathpzc{T} bounded above list its eigenvalues above the essential spectrum from the top, and the paragraphs below define these terms for a general 𝒯\mathpzc{T}.

Self-adjoint operators.

A linear operator 𝒯\mathpzc{T} on a dense domain D⁡(𝒯)D(\mathpzc{T}) of a Hilbert space is bounded if ‖𝒯​𝒻‖≤𝒞​‖𝒻‖\|\mathpzc{T}f\|\leq C\|f\| for a constant CC and all f∈D⁡(𝒯)f\in D(\mathpzc{T}). It is symmetric if ⟨f​𝒯​ℊ⟩=⟨𝒯​𝒻​ℊ⟩\langle f~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}g\rangle=\langle\mathpzc{T}f~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~g\rangle for all f,g∈D⁡(𝒯)f,g\in D(\mathpzc{T}), and self-adjoint if, in addition, its adjoint has the same domain, D⁡(𝒯†)=𝒟⁡(𝒯)D(\mathpzc{T}^{\dagger})=D(\mathpzc{T}).

Spectrum.

For a self-adjoint 𝒯\mathpzc{T}, the spectrum σ⁡(𝒯)\sigma(\mathpzc{T}) is the set of z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R} for which 𝒯−𝓏\mathpzc{T}-z has no bounded inverse on the Hilbert space. The discrete spectrum σdisc​(𝒯)\sigma_{\mathrm{disc}}(\mathpzc{T}) is the set of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, and the essential spectrum is σess(𝒯):=σ(𝒯)∖σdisc(𝒯)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sigma(\mathpzc{T})\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm{disc}}(\mathpzc{T}).

Spectral theorem.

By the spectral theorem in projection-valued-measure form [29, Theorem VIII.6], a self-adjoint 𝒯\mathpzc{T} satisfies 𝒯=∫𝓏​𝑑𝒫​𝒯​(𝓏)\mathpzc{T}=\int z\,dP{T}(z), where the spectral projection P​T​(B)P{T}(B) of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} onto a Borel set B⊂ℝB\subset\mathbb{R} is an orthogonal projection. It vanishes when BB is disjoint from σ⁡(𝒯)\sigma(\mathpzc{T}), and P​T​({z})P{T}(\{z\}) projects onto the eigenspace of an eigenvalue zz [29, pp. 236 and 264, Theorem VIII.5(e)]. For ψ∈D⁡(𝒯)\psi\in D(\mathpzc{T}) this gives ⟨ψ​𝒯​ψ⟩=∫𝓏​𝒹​νψ​(𝓏)\langle\psi~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}\psi\rangle=\int z\,d\nu_{\psi}(z) with the spectral measure νψ(B):=∥PT(B)ψ∥2\nu_{\psi}(B)\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\|P{T}(B)\psi\|^{2}.

Min–max values.

For a self-adjoint 𝒯\mathpzc{T} bounded above and j≥1j\geq 1, the min–max values

μj:=sup𝒱⊂D⁡(𝒯),dim𝒱=𝒿minψ∈𝒱,‖ψ‖=1⟨ψ𝒯ψ⟩\displaystyle\mu_{j}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sup_{\mathcal{V}\subset D(\mathpzc{T}),\,\dim\mathcal{V}=j}\ \min_{\psi\in\mathcal{V},\,\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}\psi\rangle (7)

satisfy μ1≥μ2≥⋯\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\cdots. By the min–max principle for −𝒯-\mathpzc{T}, which is bounded below [28, Theorem XIII.1], the μj\mu_{j} greater than supσess​(𝒯)\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}) are the eigenvalues of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} greater than this value, in decreasing order and counted with multiplicity, and every other μj\mu_{j} equals supσess​(𝒯)\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}).

D.1.3 The molecular Hamiltonian on ℋ\mathscr{H}

The molecular Hamiltonian ℋ\mathpzc{H} is self-adjoint on ℋ\mathscr{H}, so it has a real spectrum.

The non-relativistic electronic Coulomb Hamiltonian (cf. Section 2)

ℋ=−12∑𝒾=1𝓃𝖾𝗅∇𝐫𝒾2−∑𝒾=1𝓃𝖾𝗅∑ℐ=1𝓃𝗇𝗎𝒵ℐ‖𝐫𝒾−𝐑ℐ‖+∑1≤𝒾<𝒿≤𝓃𝖾𝗅1‖𝐫𝒾−𝐫𝒿‖\displaystyle\mathpzc{H}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}\nabla_{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}\sum_{I=1}^{{n_{\mathsf{nu}}}}\frac{Z_{I}}{\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}\|}+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}\frac{1}{\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}\|}

is unbounded but self-adjoint on L2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}) with the Sobolev space H2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}) as its dense domain, by the Kato–Rellich theorem [16], since the Coulomb potential satisfies the Kato smallness condition with respect to the kinetic operator.

The restriction of ℋ\mathpzc{H} to D(ℋ):=ℋ2(ℝ3​𝓃𝖾𝗅)∩ℋD(\mathpzc{H})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}})\cap\mathscr{H} is self-adjoint on ℋ\mathscr{H}, because ℋ\mathpzc{H} commutes with the exchange of two same-spin electrons and the antisymmetrizer maps H2​(ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅)H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}) into itself, which also makes D⁡(ℋ)D(\mathpzc{H}) dense in ℋ\mathscr{H}. We work with 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H} on D⁡(𝒯)=𝒟⁡(ℋ)D(\mathpzc{T})=D(\mathpzc{H}) throughout, and every function on which 𝒯\mathpzc{T} acts is taken in D⁡(𝒯)D(\mathpzc{T}) without further mention.

D.1.4 Spectrum and bound states

On ℋ\mathscr{H}, the spectrum of ℋ\mathpzc{H} consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity below the ionization threshold Σ\Sigma and the essential spectrum σess​(ℋ)=[Σ,∞)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{H})=[\Sigma,\infty) above it. On each ℋ(S)\mathscr{H}^{(S)}, the Hunziker–van Winter–Zhislin (HVZ) theorem [12, 41, 28] in its form for a fixed total spin [40] gives the essential spectrum [ΣS,∞)[\Sigma_{S},\infty), where ΣS\Sigma_{S} is the lowest energy of the (n𝖾𝗅−1)({n_{\mathsf{el}}}{-}1)-electron system with total spin S−12S-\frac{1}{2} or S+12S+\frac{1}{2}. Since ℋ\mathscr{H} is the finite orthogonal sum of the ℋ(S)\mathscr{H}^{(S)}, each left invariant by ℋ\mathpzc{H} (Appendix D.1.1), the essential spectrum on ℋ\mathscr{H} is the union of these intervals, [Σ,∞)[\Sigma,\infty) with Σ=minS⁡ΣS\Sigma=\min_{S}\Sigma_{S}, and below Σ\Sigma the discrete spectrum is the union of those on the ℋ(S)\mathscr{H}^{(S)}. The threshold Σ\Sigma is the lower of the ground-state energies of the two (n𝖾𝗅−1)({n_{\mathsf{el}}}{-}1)-electron systems obtained by removing one spin-up or one spin-down electron to infinity.

The eigenfunctions of ℋ\mathpzc{H} in ℋ\mathscr{H} are the bound states, and they span only part of ℋ\mathscr{H}. The energies of the bound states below Σ\Sigma form the discrete spectrum, and these states are localized near the nuclei. The essential spectrum [Σ,∞)[\Sigma,\infty) contains the energies of scattering states, which have at least one electron at infinity and whose solutions of ℋ​ψ=ℰ​ψ\mathpzc{H}\psi=E\psi lie outside ℋ\mathscr{H}. It can also contain eigenvalues: a bound state of total spin SS with energy between Σ\Sigma and ΣS\Sigma_{S} is discrete on ℋ(S)\mathscr{H}^{(S)} and embedded in the essential spectrum on ℋ\mathscr{H}. The orthogonal complement of the closed span of the bound states, the continuous spectral subspace, holds square-integrable states such as a wave packet of an electron moving away from the nuclei. The orthogonal complement of the bound states below Σ\Sigma, the essential spectral subspace, contains the continuous spectral subspace and the bound states with energies from Σ\Sigma upward.

We assume that 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H} has at least KK discrete eigenvalues separated from the essential spectrum:

μ1≥μ2≥⋯≥μK>supσess​(𝒯).\displaystyle\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{K}>\sup\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}). (8)

Since supσess​(𝒯)=−Σ\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T})=-\Sigma, this is the existence of at least KK bound states below Σ\Sigma, which holds for all systems in our experiments. The number of bound states below Σ\Sigma depends on the system; neutral atoms and positive ions have infinitely many by Zhislin’s theorem [40].

D.2 The LoRA objective for an unbounded operator

The LoRA objective of any trial functions f1,…,fKf_{1},\ldots,f_{K} is the Hilbert–Schmidt objective of the projected operator 𝒯𝒱:=𝒫𝒱𝒯𝒫𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=P_{\mathcal{V}}\,\mathpzc{T}\,P_{\mathcal{V}}, an operator of finite rank, where P𝒱P_{\mathcal{V}} is the orthogonal projection onto 𝒱:=span{f1,…,fK}\mathcal{V}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathrm{span}\{f_{1},\ldots,f_{K}\}; this holds also for the unbounded molecular 𝒯\mathpzc{T}.

Hilbert–Schmidt operators.

A bounded operator on ℋ\mathscr{H} is Hilbert–Schmidt (HS) if ∥𝒯∥𝖧𝖲2:=∑𝓃∥𝒯ℯ𝓃∥2<∞\|\mathpzc{T}\|_{\mathsf{HS}}^{2}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\sum_{n}\|\mathpzc{T}e_{n}\|^{2}<\infty for an orthonormal basis (en)(e_{n}) of ℋ\mathscr{H}, a sum that does not depend on the basis, and finite-rank if its range is finite-dimensional; a finite-rank operator is HS.

The body’s identity ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(f1:K)=∥𝒯−∑𝓀𝒻𝓀⟩⟨𝒻𝓀∥𝖧𝖲2−∥𝒯∥𝖧𝖲2\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})=\|\mathpzc{T}-\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\|_{\mathsf{HS}}^{2}-\|\mathpzc{T}\|_{\mathsf{HS}}^{2} assumes 𝒯\mathpzc{T} to be HS, which fails for molecular 𝒯\mathpzc{T}. The objective itself is defined for any f1,…,fKf_{1},\ldots,f_{K}, since the matrix elements ⟨fk​𝒯​𝒻ℓ⟩\langle f_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}f_{\ell}\rangle are finite. Like the Rayleigh quotient, which evaluates 𝒯\mathpzc{T} on its trial function alone, the objective depends on 𝒯\mathpzc{T} only through these matrix elements, that is, through 𝒯\mathpzc{T} on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The projected operator 𝒯𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}} is finite-rank, hence HS, and has the same matrix elements, ⟨fk​𝒯​𝒻ℓ⟩=⟨𝒻𝓀​𝒯𝒱​𝒻ℓ⟩\langle f_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}f_{\ell}\rangle=\langle f_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}f_{\ell}\rangle, so the identity holds exactly for 𝒯𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}:

ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(f1:K)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) =∥∑k=1Kfk⟩⟨fk−𝒯𝒱∥𝖧𝖲2−∥𝒯𝒱∥𝖧𝖲2.\displaystyle=\biggl\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}-\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\biggr\|_{\mathsf{HS}}^{2}-\|\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\|_{\mathsf{HS}}^{2}. (9)

Within a fixed 𝒱\mathcal{V}, minimizing ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}} is therefore the best positive-semidefinite (PSD) rank-KK approximation of 𝒯𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}, and the global minimization also moves 𝒱\mathcal{V}.

D.3 Global minimizers of 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}

Theorem D.1 (Global minimizers of 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}).

Let 𝒯\mathpzc{T} be self-adjoint and bounded above on ℋ\mathscr{H}, with the min–max values μj\mu_{j} of Eq. (7), and assume

μK>max⁡(supσess​(𝒯), 0).\displaystyle\mu_{K}>\max\bigl(\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}),\,0\bigr). (10)

Then μ1≥⋯≥μK\mu_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{K} are the top KK eigenvalues of 𝒯\mathpzc{T}, counted with multiplicity, and

minψ1:K≠0,λ1:K∈ℝ≥0K𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:K,λ1:K)=−∑k=1Kμk2.\displaystyle\min_{\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}\neq 0,\ \lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{K}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})=-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{k}^{2}.

Every minimizer satisfies

∑k=1Kλkψk⟩⟨ψk⟨ψk​ψk⟩=∑k=1Kμkφk⟩⟨φk\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\frac{\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}}{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\varphi_{k}\rangle\langle\varphi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}

for some orthonormal φ1:K\varphi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} with 𝒯​φ𝓀=μ𝓀​φ𝓀\mathpzc{T}\varphi_{k}=\mu_{k}\varphi_{k}. If moreover μK>μK+1\mu_{K}>\mu_{K+1}, this operator is the same for every minimizer: it is the weighted spectral projector of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} onto its top-KK eigenspace.

The min–max formula defines μj\mu_{j} for every self-adjoint 𝒯\mathpzc{T} bounded above, including the operator with the spin penalty of Appendix D.3.3, so Eq. (10) can be stated for any such 𝒯\mathpzc{T}; the first claim is the min–max principle of Appendix D.1.2, since μK>supσess​(𝒯)\mu_{K}>\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T}). For 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H}, supσess​(𝒯)=−Σ\sup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(\mathpzc{T})=-\Sigma with the ionization threshold Σ≤0\Sigma\leq 0 of Appendix D.1.4, so Eq. (10) reduces to Eq. (8).

D.3.1 Two lemmas

The proof uses two lemmas, with 𝒯\mathpzc{T} and μj\mu_{j} as in Theorem D.1 and Eq. (10) assumed. The first is the lower bound, through the projected operator 𝒯𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}} of Appendix D.2. For a finite-rank self-adjoint SS, write S+S_{+} for its positive part, and (x)+:=max(x,0)(x)_{+}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\max(x,0).

D.3.2 Proof of Theorem D.1
Proof of Theorem D.1.

Write fk=λk​ψk/‖ψk‖f_{k}=\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}\,\psi_{k}/\|\psi_{k}\|, so that 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:K,λ1:K)=ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(f1:K)\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) by the definition of 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}} in Section 3.2. The operator of the theorem is then ∑kλkψk⟩⟨ψk⟨ψk​ψk⟩=∑kfk⟩⟨fk=A𝒱\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\tfrac{\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}}{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle}=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}=A_{\mathcal{V}}, with A𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}} as in Lemma D.1.

Minimum. Lemma D.1 gives ℒ𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(f1:K)≥−∑kμk2\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(f_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})\geq-\sum_{k}\mu_{k}^{2}, and fk=μk​φkf_{k}=\sqrt{\mu_{k}}\,\varphi_{k} for orthonormal eigenfunctions 𝒯​φ𝓀=μ𝓀​φ𝓀\mathpzc{T}\varphi_{k}=\mu_{k}\varphi_{k}, given by ψk=φk\psi_{k}=\varphi_{k} and λk=μk\lambda_{k}=\mu_{k}, attains it, so a minimizer exists.

Form of every minimizer. Let (ψ1:K,λ1:K)(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) be a minimizer, so that its f1:Kf_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} attains the minimum and both inequalities of Lemma D.1 are tight: dim𝒱=K\dim\mathcal{V}=K, 𝒯𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}} has the eigenvalues μ1,…,μK\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{K} on 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and A𝒱=(𝒯𝒱)+A_{\mathcal{V}}=(\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}})_{+}. We show that A𝒱=𝒯𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}}=\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}. Let φ1:K\varphi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} be an orthonormal basis of 𝒱\mathcal{V} with 𝒯𝒱​φ𝒿=μ𝒿​φ𝒿\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\varphi_{j}=\mu_{j}\varphi_{j}; we show 𝒯​φ𝒿=μ𝒿​φ𝒿\mathpzc{T}\varphi_{j}=\mu_{j}\varphi_{j} by induction on jj. If this holds for φ1:j−1\varphi_{1\mathchar 58\relax j-1}, then φj\varphi_{j} is a unit vector in WjW_{j} with ⟨φj​𝒯​φ𝒿⟩=⟨φ𝒿​𝒯𝒱​φ𝒿⟩=μ𝒿\langle\varphi_{j}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}\varphi_{j}\rangle=\langle\varphi_{j}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}\varphi_{j}\rangle=\mu_{j}, so 𝒯​φ𝒿=μ𝒿​φ𝒿\mathpzc{T}\varphi_{j}=\mu_{j}\varphi_{j} by Lemma D.2. Since μk≥μK>0\mu_{k}\geq\mu_{K}>0, 𝒯𝒱=∑𝓀μ𝓀φ𝓀⟩⟨φ𝓀\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}=\sum_{k}\mu_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\varphi_{k}\rangle\langle\varphi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} is PSD, and A𝒱=(𝒯𝒱)+=𝒯𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}}=(\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}})_{+}=\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}}.

Uniqueness. If μK>μK+1\mu_{K}>\mu_{K+1}, at most KK orthonormal eigenfunctions have eigenvalues ≥μK\geq\mu_{K}: for K+1K+1 of them, ⟨ψ​𝒯​ψ⟩\langle\psi~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}\psi\rangle of a unit ψ\psi in their span is an average of their eigenvalues, hence ≥μK\geq\mu_{K}, so the definition of μK+1\mu_{K+1} gives μK+1≥μK\mu_{K+1}\geq\mu_{K}. 𝒱\mathcal{V} is then the top-KK eigenspace, and A𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}} is the same for every minimizer. If μK=μK+1\mu_{K}=\mu_{K+1}, 𝒱\mathcal{V} contains the eigenfunctions with eigenvalues above μK\mu_{K} and a subspace of ker⁡(𝒯−μ𝒦)\ker(\mathpzc{T}-\mu_{K}) of the remaining dimension; the minimum and the eigenvalues of A𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}} do not depend on this choice, while A𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}} itself does. ∎

D.3.3 Remarks
Nonnegative scale parameters.

The proof uses λk≥0\lambda_{k}\geq 0 in step (b) of Lemma D.1, where A𝒱=∑kfk⟩⟨fkA_{\mathcal{V}}=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} is PSD. Over λk<0\lambda_{k}<0, 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}} is unbounded below, since 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H} is unbounded below.

Spin penalty.

The spin penalty of Section 4.1 replaces ℋ\mathpzc{H} by ℋ+𝒮^2\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2}; on ℋ\mathscr{H} the total-spin operator S^2\hat{S}^{2} is bounded and commutes with ℋ\mathpzc{H}, so 𝒯=−(ℋ+𝒮^2)\mathpzc{T}=-(\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2}) is self-adjoint and bounded above, its eigenfunctions are those of ℋ\mathpzc{H} with each level raised by S⁡(S+1)S(S{+}1), and the theorem and Corollary D.1 apply to it.

Relation to Theorem C.5 of Ryu et al. [30].

Theorem D.1 holds for every self-adjoint 𝒯\mathpzc{T} bounded above under Eq. (10), because it applies Eckart–Young to the finite-rank 𝒯𝒱\mathpzc{T}_{\mathcal{V}} (Lemma D.1) and finds the eigenfunctions through the min–max values (Lemma D.2). Theorem C.5 of Ryu et al. [30] assumes an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions of 𝒯\mathpzc{T}. The essential spectrum (−∞,−Σ](-\infty,-\Sigma] of −ℋ-\mathpzc{H} contains the continuous spectrum of the scattering states, whose solutions of the eigenvalue equation lie outside ℋ\mathscr{H}. The eigenfunctions of −ℋ-\mathpzc{H} therefore span a proper subspace of ℋ\mathscr{H} (Appendix D.1.4). A trial function fkf_{k} has, in general, a component outside this subspace that an expansion of fkf_{k} in eigenfunctions misses. In exchange, Theorem D.1 requires μK>0\mu_{K}>0, while Theorem C.5 also covers an operator with only r<Kr<K positive eigenvalues.

Scale parameters at a minimizer.

With fk=λk​ψk/‖ψk‖f_{k}=\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}\,\psi_{k}/\|\psi_{k}\| as in the proof, the objective depends on f1:Kf_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} only through A𝒱=∑kfk⟩⟨fkA_{\mathcal{V}}=\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}. For a minimizer with A𝒱=∑jμjφj⟩⟨φjA_{\mathcal{V}}=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\varphi_{j}\rangle\langle\varphi_{j}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}, the fkf_{k} are exactly fk=∑j=1KUj​k​μj​φjf_{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{K}U_{jk}\sqrt{\mu_{j}}\,\varphi_{j} with UU a K×KK\times K unitary, because two families of KK vectors with the same rank-KK operator ∑kfk⟩⟨fk\sum_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} differ by a unitary. Then λk=‖fk‖2=∑jUj​k2​μj\lambda_{k}=\|f_{k}\|^{2}=\sum_{j}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}U_{jk}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}\mu_{j}. The joint minimum fixes the eigenvalues of A𝒱A_{\mathcal{V}} but not each λk\lambda_{k}, which equals μk\mu_{k} only if UU does not mix distinct eigenvalues. Corollary D.1 in Appendix D.4 shows that sequential nesting removes this freedom.

D.4 Fixed point of sequential nesting

This section treats sequential nesting once more, through its objective. The fixed point of sequential nesting is the ordered eigenpairs, up to a rotation within each degenerate level (Corollary D.1), while the joint minimum of Theorem D.1 fixes the states only up to a rotation among all KK of them. The sequential nesting gradient derived in Appendix E.1.4 can be read as KK optimizations, one per network: network kk minimizes the order-kk objective 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k}) over its own arguments, with the networks below it held fixed, and the corollary characterizes the fixed point of these KK optimizations.

If networks 1,…,k−11,\ldots,k-1 hold the top k−1k-1 eigenpairs, the order-kk objective minimized over λk\lambda_{k} depends on ψk\psi_{k} only through q⁡(ψ^k)=⟨ψ^k​𝒯​ψ^𝓀⟩−∑ℓ<𝓀μℓ​⟨ψ^ℓ​ψ^𝓀⟩2q(\hat{\psi}_{k})=\langle\hat{\psi}_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{T}\hat{\psi}_{k}\rangle-\sum_{\ell<k}\mu_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\langle\hat{\psi}_{\ell}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\hat{\psi}_{k}\rangle\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2} with ψ^k=ψk/‖ψk‖\hat{\psi}_{k}=\psi_{k}/\|\psi_{k}\|. This qq is largest exactly at the eigenfunctions of eigenvalue μk\mu_{k} orthogonal to the lower networks (Lemma D.2). Induction on kk then gives each network one eigenfunction and λk=μk\lambda_{k}=\mu_{k}.

Corollary D.1 (Fixed point of sequential nesting).

Assume Eq. (10), and let (ψ1:K,λ1:K)(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K}) be such that, for each k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, (ψk,λk)(\psi_{k},\lambda_{k}) minimizes the order-kk objective 𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k}) over its own arguments with (ψ1:k−1,λ1:k−1)(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k-1},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k-1}) held fixed. Then for every kk, ψk\psi_{k} is an eigenfunction of 𝒯\mathpzc{T} with eigenvalue μk\mu_{k}, orthogonal to ψ1:k−1\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k-1}, and λk=μk\lambda_{k}=\mu_{k}. The statement also holds at μK=μK+1\mu_{K}=\mu_{K+1}, and within a degenerate level ψk\psi_{k} may be any such eigenfunction.

By induction on kk.
