With fℓ=λℓ​ψ^ℓf_{\ell}=\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell}}\,\hat{\psi}_{\ell}, the order-kk objective is −2∑ℓ≤k⟨fℓ𝒯𝒻ℓ⟩+∑ℓ,𝓂≤𝓀⟨𝒻ℓ𝒻𝓂⟩2-2\sum_{\ell\leq k}\langle f_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\mathpzc{T}f_{\ell}\rangle+\sum_{\ell,m\leq k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\langle f_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{m}\rangle\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}, and its terms with fkf_{k} are −2​⟨fk​𝒯​𝒻𝓀⟩-2\langle f_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\mathpzc{T}f_{k}\rangle, the cross terms 2​∑ℓ<k⟨fℓ​fk⟩22\sum_{\ell<k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\langle f_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}f_{k}\rangle\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2} and the diagonal term ‖fk‖4=λk2\|f_{k}\|^{4}=\lambda_{k}^{2}. Their sum is −2​λk​q​(ψ^k)+λk2-2\lambda_{k}\,q(\hat{\psi}_{k})+\lambda_{k}^{2} with

q(ψ^):=⟨ψ^𝒯ψ^⟩−∑ℓ<𝓀μℓ⟨ψ^ℓψ^⟩2=⟨(1−𝒫)ψ^𝒯(1−𝒫)ψ^⟩,\displaystyle q(\hat{\psi})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\langle\hat{\psi}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\mathpzc{T}\hat{\psi}\rangle-\sum_{\ell<k}\mu_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\langle\hat{\psi}_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\hat{\psi}\rangle\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}=\langle(1-P)\hat{\psi}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\mathpzc{T}(1-P)\hat{\psi}\rangle,

where the last equality holds because 𝒯\mathpzc{T} maps the span of ψ^1:k−1\hat{\psi}_{1\mathchar 58\relax k-1} into itself. Over λk≥0\lambda_{k}\geq 0 the minimum is −q​(ψ^k)+2-q(\hat{\psi}_{k})_{+}^{2}, at λk=q​(ψ^k)+\lambda_{k}=q(\hat{\psi}_{k})_{+}, so ψ^k\hat{\psi}_{k} maximizes qq over unit vectors. For q⁡(ψ^k)>0q(\hat{\psi}_{k})>0 this λk\lambda_{k} is the analytic update of Eq. (6) (Appendix E.2) with λℓ=μℓ\lambda_{\ell}=\mu_{\ell} for ℓ<k\ell<k, so the corollary also covers λk\lambda_{k} set by that update. By Lemma D.2, q⁡(ψ^)≤μk​‖(1−P)​ψ^‖2≤μkq(\hat{\psi})\leq\mu_{k}\|(1-P)\hat{\psi}\|^{2}\leq\mu_{k}, and since μk≥μK>0\mu_{k}\geq\mu_{K}>0 both bounds are attained exactly when P​ψ^=0P\hat{\psi}=0 and 𝒯​ψ^=μ𝓀​ψ^\mathpzc{T}\hat{\psi}=\mu_{k}\hat{\psi}; such a ψ^\hat{\psi} exists because μ1:K\mu_{1\mathchar 58\relax K} are counted with multiplicity. Hence ψ^k\hat{\psi}_{k} is an eigenfunction of eigenvalue μk\mu_{k} orthogonal to ψ^1:k−1\hat{\psi}_{1\mathchar 58\relax k-1}, and λk=μk\lambda_{k}=\mu_{k}. ∎

Appendix E Deferred proofs

This section derives the gradient expressions and the eigenvalue update that the main text states without proof.

E.1 Gradient expressions

E.1.1 Proof of Eq. (1) (VMC gradient)

The gradient expression of the VMC Rayleigh quotient can be immediately derived from the following lemma.

Lemma E.1.

For a symmetric operator 𝒪\mathpzc{O},

∇θ⟨ψθ​𝒪​ψθ⟩⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩\displaystyle\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle} =2​Re(𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[𝒪​ψθ​(𝐱)ψθ​(𝐱)​∇θ​log⁡ψθ∗​(𝐱)]).\displaystyle=2\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\biggl(\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\biggl[\frac{\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}{\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})\biggr]\biggr).
Proof.

The inner product between a vector-valued function and a scalar function denotes the coordinate-wise operation. By the chain rule, the commutativity of 𝒪\mathpzc{O} with ∇θ\nabla_{\theta}, and the symmetry of 𝒪\mathpzc{O},

∇θ⟨ψθ​𝒪​ψθ⟩=2​Re⟨∇θψθ​𝒪​ψθ⟩=2​‖ψθ‖2​Re𝔼𝓅θ​(𝐱)​[𝒪​ψθ​(𝐱)ψθ​(𝐱)​∇θ​log⁡ψθ∗​(𝐱)],\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\theta}\rangle=2\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\langle\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\theta}\rangle=2\|\psi_{\theta}\|^{2}\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\!\biggl[\frac{\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}{\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})\biggr],

where the second equality multiplies and divides by ψθ​(𝐱)2/‖ψθ‖2=pθ​(𝐱)\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}/\|\psi_{\theta}\|^{2}=p_{\theta}({\bf x}). Dividing both sides by ⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩=‖ψθ‖2\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle=\|\psi_{\theta}\|^{2} gives the claim. ∎

Proof of Eq. (1).

Consider

∇θℒ​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta) =∇θ⟨ψθ​ℋ​ψθ⟩⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩−⟨ψθ​ℋ​ψθ⟩​∇θ⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩2\displaystyle=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle}-\frac{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\theta}\rangle\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle^{2}}
=∇θ⟨ψθ​ℋ​ψθ⟩⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩−ℒ⁡(θ)​∇θ⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩⟨ψθ​ψθ⟩\displaystyle=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle}-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\theta}\rangle}
=(a)2​Re(𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[ℋ​ψθ​(𝐱)ψθ​(𝐱)​∇θ​log​ψθ∗​(𝐱)]−ℒ⁡(θ)​𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[∇θ​log​ψθ∗​(𝐱)])\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\displaystyle{(a)}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\textstyle{(a)}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\scriptstyle{(a)}$\hss}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\scriptscriptstyle{(a)}$\hss}}}}{{=}}2\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\biggl(\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\Bigl[\frac{\mathpzc{H}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}{\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})}\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})\Bigr]-\mathcal{L}(\theta)\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\Bigl[\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})\Bigr]\biggr)
=2​Re(𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[(ℰθ​(𝐱)−𝔼pθ​(𝐱)​[ℰθ​(𝐱)])​∇θ​log⁡ψθ∗​(𝐱)]).\displaystyle=2\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}\Bigl[(\mathcal{E}_{\theta}({\bf x})-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\theta}({\bf x})}[\mathcal{E}_{\theta}({\bf x})])\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})\Bigr]\Bigr).

Here, (a) follows from Lemma E.1. When ψθ​(𝐱)∈ℝ\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\in\mathbb{R} for any 𝐱{\bf x}, note that

∇θlogψθ∗(𝐱)=∇θ(logψθ(𝐱)+logsgn(ψθ(𝐱)))=∇θlogψθ(𝐱)+∇θlogsgn(ψθ(𝐱)).\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})=\nabla_{\theta}(\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}+\log\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})))=\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}+\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})).

Here, taking log\log as the complex logarithm with its branch cut along the negative imaginary axis, ∇θ​log​sgn(ψθ​(𝐱))\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})) is well defined and equals 00 for almost every 𝐱{\bf x}, since sgn(ψθ​(𝐱))∈{−1,1}\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(\psi_{\theta}({\bf x}))\in\{-1,1\} is locally constant in θ\theta wherever ψθ​(𝐱)≠0\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\neq 0. Thus we can conclude ∇θ​log​ψθ∗​(𝐱)=∇θ​log​ψθ​(𝐱)\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*}({\bf x})=\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}, and numerically we ignore this sign term and differentiate log⁡ψθ\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} alone. This gives Eq. (1) with ∇θ​log​ψθ\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\theta}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} in place of ∇θ​log​ψθ∗\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}^{*} for a real-valued ansatz. ∎

E.1.2 Derivation of the LoRA gradient
Lemma E.2.

Define

Γk​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle\Gamma_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} :=∇θ⟨ψk​𝒪​ψℓ⟩⟨ψk​ψk⟩.\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle}.

Then, we have

∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} =Γk​ℓ𝒪−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Γk​kℐ.\displaystyle=\Gamma_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\Gamma_{kk}^{\mathpzc{I}}. (11)
Proof.

The quotient rule on 𝖱k​ℓ𝒪=⟨ψk​𝒪​ψℓ⟩/⟨ψ𝓀​ψ𝓀⟩\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}=\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}\rangle/\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle gives ∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪=Γk​ℓ𝒪−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Γk​kℐ\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}=\Gamma_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\,\Gamma_{kk}^{\mathpzc{I}}. ∎

Lemma E.3.

Define

Δk​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle\Delta_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} :=⟨∇θψk​𝒪​ψℓ⟩⟨ψk​ψk⟩=𝔼pk​(𝐱)[𝒪​ψℓ​(𝐱)ψk​(𝐱)∇θlogψk∗(𝐱)].\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\frac{\langle\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}({\bf x})}\biggl[\frac{\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}({\bf x})}{\psi_{k}({\bf x})}\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{k}^{*}({\bf x})\biggr].

Then, for a symmetric operator 𝒪\mathpzc{O}, we have

Γk​ℓ𝒪=Δk​ℓ𝒪+‖ψℓ‖2‖ψk‖2​(Δℓ​k​O)∗\displaystyle\Gamma_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}=\Delta_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}+\frac{\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}}(\Delta_{\ell k}{O})^{*}

In particular, when ℓ=k\ell=k, we have Δk​kℐ=γk\Delta_{kk}^{\mathpzc{I}}=\gamma_{k} and

Γk​kℐ=γk+γk∗,\Gamma_{kk}^{\mathpzc{I}}=\gamma_{k}+\gamma_{k}^{*},

where we define

γk\displaystyle\gamma_{k} :=𝔼pk[∇θlogψk∗].\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}\bigl[\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{k}^{*}\bigr].
Proof.

The product rule gives ∇θ⟨ψk​𝒪​ψℓ⟩=⟨∇θψ𝓀​𝒪​ψℓ⟩+⟨ψ𝓀​𝒪​∇θψℓ⟩\nabla_{\theta}\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}\rangle=\langle\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}\rangle+\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{\ell}\rangle, and since 𝒪\mathpzc{O} is symmetric the second term is ⟨∇θψℓ​𝒪​ψ𝓀⟩∗\langle\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{\ell}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\mathpzc{O}\psi_{k}\rangle^{*}; dividing by ⟨ψk​ψk⟩\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle gives the identity. Setting ℓ=k\ell=k and 𝒪=ℐ\mathpzc{O}=\mathpzc{I} in the definition of Δk​ℓ𝒪\Delta_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} gives Δk​kℐ=γk\Delta_{kk}^{\mathpzc{I}}=\gamma_{k}. ∎

The gradient identity used to assemble Eq. (4) follows from the lemma below.

Lemma E.4.

Define

Δ~k​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} :=Covpk(𝒪​ψℓψk,∇θlogψk∗)=Δk​ℓ𝒪−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪γk.\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathop{\rm Cov}\nolimits_{p_{k}}\biggl(\frac{\mathpzc{O}\psi_{\ell}}{\psi_{k}},\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{k}^{*}\biggr)=\Delta_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{k}. (12)

Then,

∇θ𝖱k​k𝒯=Δ~k​k𝒯+(Δ~k​k𝒯)∗=2​Re(Δ~k​k𝒯).\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}=\tilde{\Delta}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}+(\tilde{\Delta}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}})^{*}=2\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits(\tilde{\Delta}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}).

For a symmetric operator 𝒪\mathpzc{O}, we have

∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​𝖱ℓ​kℐ\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}} =𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Δ~ℓ​k​I+(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​Δ~k​ℓ​I)∗+𝖱ℓ​kℐ​Δ~k​ℓ​O+(𝖱k​ℓℐ​Δ~ℓ​k​O)∗\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{I}+(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{I})^{*}+\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{O}+(\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{O})^{*}
=2​Re{𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Δ~ℓ​k​I+𝖱ℓ​kℐ​Δ~k​ℓ​O}if ​𝒪=ℐ.\displaystyle=2\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits\Bigl\{\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{I}+\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{O}\Bigr\}\quad\text{if }\mathpzc{O}=\mathpzc{I}.
Proof.

Continuing from Eq. (11),

∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} =Γk​ℓ𝒪−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Γk​kℐ\displaystyle=\Gamma_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\Gamma_{kk}^{\mathpzc{I}}
=Δk​ℓ𝒪+‖ψℓ‖2‖ψk‖2​(Δℓ​k​O)∗−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​(γk+γk∗)\displaystyle=\Delta_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}+\frac{\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}}(\Delta_{\ell k}{O})^{*}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}(\gamma_{k}+\gamma_{k}^{*})
=(Δk​ℓ𝒪−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​γk)+‖ψℓ‖2‖ψk‖2​(Δℓ​k​O−𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​γℓ)∗+‖ψℓ‖2‖ψk‖2​(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​γℓ)∗−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​γk∗\displaystyle=(\Delta_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{k})+\frac{\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}}(\Delta_{\ell k}{O}-\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{\ell})^{*}+\frac{\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}}(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{\ell})^{*}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{k}^{*}
=Δ~k​ℓ​O+‖ψℓ‖2‖ψk‖2​(Δ~ℓ​k​O)∗+‖ψℓ‖2‖ψk‖2​(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​γℓ)∗−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​γk∗.\displaystyle=\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{O}+\frac{\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}}(\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{O})^{*}+\frac{\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}}(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{\ell})^{*}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{k}^{*}.

This leads to:

𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​∇θ𝖱ℓ​kℐ\displaystyle\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}} =𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Δ~ℓ​k​I+(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​Δ~k​ℓ​I)∗+(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​𝖱k​ℓℐ​γk)∗−𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​𝖱ℓ​kℐ​γℓ∗,\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{I}+(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{I})^{*}+(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\gamma_{k})^{*}-\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\gamma_{\ell}^{*},
𝖱ℓ​kℐ​∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}} =𝖱ℓ​kℐ​Δ~k​ℓ​O+(𝖱k​ℓℐ​Δ~ℓ​k​O)∗+(𝖱k​ℓℐ​𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​γℓ)∗−𝖱ℓ​kℐ​𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​γk∗.\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{O}+(\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{O})^{*}+(\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{\ell})^{*}-\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\gamma_{k}^{*}.

Summing them up, we get

∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​𝖱ℓ​kℐ\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}} =𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​∇θ𝖱ℓ​kℐ+𝖱ℓ​kℐ​∇θ𝖱k​ℓ𝒪\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}+\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\nabla_{\theta}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}
=(𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Δ~ℓ​k​I+(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​Δ~k​ℓ​I)∗+𝖱ℓ​kℐ​Δ~k​ℓ​O+(𝖱k​ℓℐ​Δ~ℓ​k​O)∗)\displaystyle=\Bigl(\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{I}+(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{I})^{*}+\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{O}+(\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{O})^{*}\Bigr)
+((𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​𝖱k​ℓℐ)∗−𝖱ℓ​kℐ​𝖱k​ℓ𝒪)​(γk∗+γℓ∗)\displaystyle\quad+\Bigl((\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}})^{*}-\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\Bigr)(\gamma_{k}^{*}+\gamma_{\ell}^{*})
=𝖱k​ℓ𝒪​Δ~ℓ​k​I+(𝖱ℓ​k𝒪​Δ~k​ℓ​I)∗+𝖱ℓ​kℐ​Δ~k​ℓ​O+(𝖱k​ℓℐ​Δ~ℓ​k​O)∗.\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{I}+(\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{O}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{I})^{*}+\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}{O}+(\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{\ell k}{O})^{*}.

This concludes the proof. ∎

E.1.3 Final gradient expression for implementation

Recall that Δ~𝒪\tilde{\Delta}^{\mathpzc{O}} is defined in Eq. (12). For simplicity, we assume real ansatzes without loss of generality. Let θk\theta_{k} denote the parameters of network kk; with ∇θk\nabla_{\theta_{k}} in place of ∇θ\nabla_{\theta} in Eq. (12), Δ~i​j𝒪=0\tilde{\Delta}_{ij}^{\mathpzc{O}}=0 for i≠ki\neq k.

Theorem E.1 (LoRA gradient).
{∇θk𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)=−4​λk​Δ~k​k𝒯+4​∑ℓ=1kλk​λℓ​𝖱ℓ​kℐ​Δ~k​ℓℐ,∂λk𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)=−2​𝖱k​k𝒯+2​∑ℓ=1kλℓ​𝖱ℓ​kℐ​𝖱k​ℓℐ.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k})&\displaystyle=-4\lambda_{k}\tilde{\Delta}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}+4\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\lambda_{k}\lambda_{\ell}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}},\\ \displaystyle\mathop{}\!\partial_{\lambda_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k})&\displaystyle=-2\mathsf{R}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\lambda_{\ell}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}.\end{cases}

Sequential nesting applies this gradient for each kk.

Surrogate objective for autograd.

To compute the centered gradient of Eq. (5) with a generic autograd, we differentiate a surrogate objective whose derivative gives this gradient. The surrogate, whose autograd derivative is twice the centered gradient, is

ℒ˘𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:K,λ1:K):=2∑k=1K𝔼pk[𝗌𝗀(gk−𝔼pk[gk])logψk],\displaystyle\breve{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax K},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax K})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=2\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}\!\bigl[\mathsf{sg}(g_{k}-\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[g_{k}])\,\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\bigr], (13)

where 𝗌𝗀\mathsf{sg} is the stop-gradient operator. The surrogate depends on θ\theta only through log⁡ψk\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}, in which it is linear, so a generic autograd differentiates it directly. In gkg_{k}, 𝖱ℓ​kℐ\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}} is estimated by its batch mean.

E.2 Derivation of the analytic eigenvalue update in Eq. (6)

We derive the closed form of Eq. (6) step by step. For each k∈[K]k\in[K], the partial derivative of the LoRA objective with respect to λk\lambda_{k} at the sequentially nested level is

⁡∂⁡∂⁡λk𝒥𝖫𝗈𝖱𝖠(ψ1:k,λ1:k)\displaystyle\frac{\mathop{}\!\partial}{\mathop{}\!\partial\lambda_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathsf{LoRA}}(\psi_{1\mathchar 58\relax k},\lambda_{1\mathchar 58\relax k}) =−2​𝖱k​k​T+2​∑ℓ=1kλℓ​𝖱k​ℓℐ​𝖱ℓ​kℐ.\displaystyle=-2\mathsf{R}_{kk}{T}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\lambda_{\ell}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}.

Setting this to zero,

λk⋆=𝖱k​k​T−∑ℓ=1k−1λℓ⋆​𝖱k​ℓℐ​𝖱ℓ​kℐ.\displaystyle\lambda_{k}^{\star}=\mathsf{R}_{kk}{T}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1}\lambda_{\ell}^{\star}\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell k}^{\mathpzc{I}}.

Solving sequentially in kk yields

λ1⋆\displaystyle\lambda_{1}^{\star} =𝖱11𝒯,\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{11}^{\mathpzc{T}},
λ2⋆\displaystyle\lambda_{2}^{\star} =𝖱22𝒯−λ1⋆​𝖱21ℐ​𝖱12ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{22}^{\mathpzc{T}}-\lambda_{1}^{\star}\mathsf{R}_{21}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{12}^{\mathpzc{I}},
λK⋆\displaystyle\lambda_{K}^{\star} =𝖱K​K𝒯−∑ℓ=1K−1λℓ⋆​𝖱K​ℓℐ​𝖱ℓ​Kℐ.\displaystyle=\mathsf{R}_{KK}^{\mathpzc{T}}-\sum_{\ell=1}^{K-1}\lambda_{\ell}^{\star}\mathsf{R}_{K\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{\ell K}^{\mathpzc{I}}.

In matrix-vector form,

𝝀⋆\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star} =diag(𝖱𝒯)−[0λ1⋆​𝖱21ℐ​𝖱12ℐλ1⋆​𝖱K,1ℐ​𝖱1,Kℐ+…+λK−1⋆​𝖱K,K−1ℐ​𝖱K−1,Kℐ]\displaystyle=\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}})-\begin{bmatrix}0\\ \lambda_{1}^{\star}\mathsf{R}_{21}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{12}^{\mathpzc{I}}\\ \vdots\\ \lambda_{1}^{\star}\mathsf{R}_{K,1}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{1,K}^{\mathpzc{I}}+\ldots+\lambda_{K-1}^{\star}\mathsf{R}_{K,K-1}^{\mathpzc{I}}\mathsf{R}_{K-1,K}^{\mathpzc{I}}\end{bmatrix}
=diag(𝖱𝒯)−(𝖬𝗌𝖾𝗊⊙(𝖱ℐ⊙(𝖱ℐ)⊺))​𝝀⋆,\displaystyle=\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}})-\bigl(\mathsf{M}^{\mathsf{seq}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}})^{\intercal})\bigr)\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star},

which rearranges to the closed form quoted in the main text:

𝝀⋆\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star} =(𝖨+𝖬𝗌𝖾𝗊⊙(𝖱ℐ⊙(𝖱ℐ)⊺))−1​diag(𝖱𝒯).\displaystyle=\bigl(\mathsf{I}+\mathsf{M}^{\mathsf{seq}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}})^{\intercal})\bigr)^{-1}\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}).

In our implementation, 𝖱𝒯\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}} and 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} in this solve are estimated by exponential moving averages (EMAs) of their per-step batch means, which smooths 𝝀⋆\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star} across steps. The EMA is warm-started: at step 11 it takes the first batch statistic itself rather than blending against an arbitrary prior x^0\hat{x}_{0}, so the smoothing starts at step 22. The gradient coefficient gkg_{k} of Eq. (5) uses the per-step batch means.

Appendix F Monte Carlo statistics

This section gives the estimates of energies and overlaps that Section 3.3 takes from the walkers.

Averages over steps.

An exponential moving average (EMA) over training steps tt of a batch statistic xtx_{t} is mt=αt​xt+(1−αt)​mt−1m_{t}=\alpha_{t}x_{t}+(1-\alpha_{t})\,m_{t-1}. The inputs 𝖱𝒯\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}} and 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} of the eigenvalue solve (Appendix E.2) and the logarithm of the norm-ratio estimate (Appendix F.2) are EMAs with αt=0.01\alpha_{t}=0.01, started at m1=x1m_{1}=x_{1}. The energies that rank the networks (Appendix G.2) are EMAs with the schedule αt=max⁡(10−3, 1/(2+t/10))\alpha_{t}=\max(10^{-3},\,1/(2+t/10)) of DeepQMC [9], which falls from 1/21/2 to 10−310^{-3} within the first ∼104{\sim}10^{4} steps.

F.1 Energy statistics

Clipping.

The local energy in Δ~k​k𝒯\tilde{\Delta}_{kk}^{\mathpzc{T}}, x=ℰk​(𝐱)x=\mathcal{E}_{k}({\bf x}) plus S^loc2​(𝐱)\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\bf x}) when the spin penalty is on (Appendix G.3), is clipped to the window [m−w​d,m+w​d][m-w\,d,\,m+w\,d] around its batch median mm, with w=10w=10 and d:=𝔼[x−m]d\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}x-m\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}]. The clipped values enter the energy term of gkg_{k} and the energy input of the eigenvalue solver.

F.2 Overlap statistics

The ratio ψℓ​(𝐱)/ψk​(𝐱)\psi_{\ell}({\bf x})/\psi_{k}({\bf x}) in Δ~k​ℓℐ\tilde{\Delta}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}} enters training unclipped, because a clip of this heavy-tailed ratio biases the overlap estimate (Appendices F.2.1 and F.2.2). The coefficient 𝖱ℓ​kℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}_{\ell k} of gkg_{k} in Eq. (5) is the unclipped batch mean of the reverse ratio ψk/ψℓ\psi_{k}/\psi_{\ell} on the walkers of ψℓ\psi_{\ell}, and the eigenvalue solve of Eq. (6) takes the EMA of the same unclipped batch means as 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}. Before these means are formed, each ratio is divided by the square root of an estimate of the norm ratio ⟨ψℓ​ψℓ⟩/⟨ψk​ψk⟩=𝔼pk​[(ψℓ/ψk)2]\langle\psi_{\ell}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\ell}\rangle/\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{k}\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[(\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k})^{2}], obtained by exponentiating an EMA (Appendix F) of the logarithm of its batch mean. This division makes the batch mean of a ratio an estimate of the normalized overlap 𝖲~k​ℓ\tilde{\mathsf{S}}_{k\ell}. The two ratios of a pair are rescaled by estimates from different chains, and the overlap term of gkg_{k} multiplies one rescaled ratio by the batch mean of the other, so this term is multiplied by a factor that is one at the exact norm ratios; the estimate could be replaced by the iterative bridge sampling of Gao et al. [6], or the rescaling removed.

F.2.1 Heavy-tail behavior of the overlap-term ratio at nodal surfaces

The ratio ψℓ​(𝐱)/ψk​(𝐱)\psi_{\ell}({\bf x})/\psi_{k}({\bf x}) at 𝐱∼pk{\bf x}\sim p_{k} has a heavy tail near the nodes of ψk\psi_{k}, and it is the per-sample integrand of the overlap term of gkg_{k} in Eq. (5). At a node of ψk\psi_{k}, ψk\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} vanishes while ψℓ\psi_{\ell} is generically nonzero, so the ratio diverges for a walker close to a node of the denominator, while its mean 𝖱k​ℓℐ\mathsf{R}_{k\ell}^{\mathpzc{I}} stays finite.

Closed-form example: Hydrogen 2​pz2p_{z} vs 2​px2p_{x}.

The simplest non-trivial pair already shows the heavy tail: take ψk=ψ2​pz\psi_{k}=\psi_{2p_{z}} as the denominator and ψℓ=ψ2​px\psi_{\ell}=\psi_{2p_{x}} as the numerator on Hydrogen. Both have the same radial factor, which cancels, so the overlap ratio reduces to the angular ratio

R⁡(𝐱)=ψ2​px​(𝐱)ψ2​pz​(𝐱)=tan⁡θ⋅cos⁡ϕ,\displaystyle R({\bf x})\;=\;\frac{\psi_{2p_{x}}({\bf x})}{\psi_{2p_{z}}({\bf x})}\;=\;\tan\theta\cdot\cos\phi,

sampled at 𝐱∼ψ2​pz2{\bf x}\sim\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{2p_{z}}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}. Setting u=cos⁡θu=\cos\theta, the squared density factorizes as 32​u2​d​u⋅12​π​d​ϕ\frac{3}{2}u^{2}\,\mathrm{d}u\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi}\,\mathrm{d}\phi, so the polar and azimuthal factors are independent. The polar tail is ℙ(tanθ>w)=(1+w2)−3/2\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\tan\theta\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}>w)=(1+w^{2})^{-3/2} exactly. Integrating over ϕ\phi and differentiating gives the closed-form density

fR​(r)=2π​1(1+r2)2,r∈ℝ,\displaystyle f_{R}(r)\;=\;\frac{2}{\pi}\,\frac{1}{(1+r^{2})^{2}},\qquad r\in\mathbb{R}, (14)

which (after the rescaling x=3​rx=\sqrt{3}\,r) is exactly Student’s tt distribution with ν=3\nu=3 degrees of freedom. The tail decays as ℙ⁡(R>t)∼4/(3​π​t3)\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}R\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}>t)\sim 4/(3\pi t^{3}) as t→∞t\to\infty, and consequently 𝔼⁡[Rp]<∞\mathbb{E}[\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}R\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{p}]<\infty if and only if p<3p<3: the per-sample overlap estimator has a finite mean and a finite variance, but its third absolute moment diverges logarithmically.

The local energy and the ratio differ in how their distributions behave as the networks converge. At an eigenstate the local energy is constant, ℰk​(𝐱)=Ek\mathcal{E}_{k}({\bf x})=E_{k} for every 𝐱{\bf x}, so its distribution under pkp_{k} shrinks to a point, every sample falls inside the clip window, and the energy clip does not act. At the eigenfunctions the ratio R=φℓ/φkR=\varphi_{\ell}/\varphi_{k} keeps the tail ℙ⁡(R>t)∼t−3\mathbb{P}(\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}R\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}>t)\sim t^{-3} of Proposition F.1 near every node of φk\varphi_{k}.

F.2.2 Measurements on trained networks

On trained networks, a clip biases the batch means of the overlap statistics by much more than it reduces their spread (Section 3.3.1). The networks trained with the unclipped ratio are close to orthogonal (Figure 2).

Long chains.

Two long Metropolis chains for each pair of networks ψk\psi_{k} and ψℓ\psi_{\ell}, run on saved checkpoints, give the reference value of 𝔼pk​[ψℓ/ψk]\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k}] and the normalized overlap of the pair. The chains sample the density proportional to ρ=ψk2+e−a​ψℓ2\rho=\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}+e^{-a}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}, so they cross the nodes of ψk\psi_{k} more often than the chain of ψk\psi_{k}. With 𝔼^ρ​[f]\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[f] the mean of ff over their walkers, we estimate

𝔼pk​[ψℓψk]=⟨ψk​ψℓ⟩‖ψk‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}\!\left[\frac{\psi_{\ell}}{\psi_{k}}\right]=\frac{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\ell}\rangle}{\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}} ≈𝔼^ρ​[ψk​ψℓ/ρ]𝔼^ρ​[ψk2/ρ],\displaystyle\approx\frac{\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[\psi_{k}\psi_{\ell}/\rho]}{\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}/\rho]},
⟨ψk​ψℓ⟩‖ψk‖​‖ψℓ‖\displaystyle\frac{\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\ell}\rangle}{\|\psi_{k}\|\,\|\psi_{\ell}\|} ≈𝔼^ρ​[ψk​ψℓ/ρ]𝔼^ρ​[ψk2/ρ]​𝔼^ρ​[ψℓ2/ρ].\displaystyle\approx\frac{\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[\psi_{k}\psi_{\ell}/\rho]}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}/\rho]\,\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{\ell}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}/\rho]}}.

Since the walkers follow ρ/Zρ\rho/Z_{\rho} with Zρ=∫ρZ_{\rho}=\int\rho, 𝔼^ρ​[f/ρ]\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{\rho}[f/\rho] tends to Zρ−1​∫fZ_{\rho}^{-1}\int f, so ZρZ_{\rho} cancels in each ratio and every aa gives the same limit. The constant aa sets only the share of walkers on ψk2\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}, ‖ψk‖2/(‖ψk‖2+e−a​‖ψℓ‖2)\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}/(\|\psi_{k}\|^{2}+e^{-a}\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}). Optimally, eae^{a} is the norm ratio ‖ψℓ‖2/‖ψk‖2\|\psi_{\ell}\|^{2}/\|\psi_{k}\|^{2} estimated from shorter chains, which makes this share about 1/21/2.

Bias of the clip (Figure 4a& 4b).

Clipping RR at a fixed number of median absolute deviations (MADs) strongly biases its batch mean; the bias remains at a width of 5050 MADs and is gone only at 100100 MADs (Figure 4b). Figure 4b shows that the bias of the clip is many times the spread across batches, even though the clip lowers this spread by removing the tail of RR. The clipped batch mean is thus a precise estimate of a shifted value. For the reverse ratio ψ5/ψ1\psi_{5}/\psi_{1} on the chain of ψ1\psi_{1}, the unclipped batch mean lies near the reference. The ratio clip lowers it to half of it or less.

We provisionally apply the ratio clip of the DeepQMC code [9] at 1010 MADs to R=ψ1/ψ5R=\psi_{1}/\psi_{5} at step 1,0001{,}000 of a Li run. The fraction of walkers beyond ss MADs in Figure 4a is the fraction a ratio clip of width ss changes. The walkers of ψ5\psi_{5} come from its training chain and from restarted chains, which cross the nodes of ψ5\psi_{5} more often. The two long chains of this pair use a=0a=0, which gives the same limit, with 4,0964{,}096 walkers each and 45,00045{,}000 steps; their walkers, resampled to p5p_{5} and then moved by 300300 Metropolis steps on p5p_{5}, start the restarted chains. Without a clip, the batch mean agrees with the long-chain reference within its spread across batches on the restarted chains and has the opposite sign on the training chain, so Figure 4b shows the restarted chains only.

The ratio at the end of training (Figure 4c& 4d).

The ratio R=ψℓ/ψkR=\psi_{\ell}/\psi_{k} keeps a heavy, power-law tail to the end of training, as the analysis of Appendix F.2.1 supports. At step 100,000100{,}000 of the seed-11 Li run, we measure the tail of each of the 9090 ratios by the fraction of the 4,0964{,}096 training walkers of ψk\psi_{k} at which RR lies more than ss MADs from its median. Proposition F.1 gives this fraction an asymptotic log-log slope of −3-3 in ss; the slopes fitted to the 9090 ratios have median −2.5-2.5 and quartiles −3.0-3.0 and −1.9-1.9.

At the end of training, where the overlaps should vanish, the ratio clip at 1010 MADs still changes the walkers of many ratios (Figure 4c) and biases their batch means. The clip window is centered on the batch median, so the clip removes more walkers on the heavier side of the tail and moves the batch mean toward the median (Figure 4d). For R=ψ4/ψ6R=\psi_{4}/\psi_{6}, the ratio whose batch mean the clip moves farthest relative to its long-chain value, the clip moves the batch mean from −0.0033-0.0033 to +0.0354+0.0354, close to the median +0.0302+0.0302, while the long chains give +0.0012±0.0006+0.0012\pm 0.0006.

Overlaps of the trained networks.

The near-orthogonality of the trained networks in Figure 2 of Section 4.3 is measured on long chains, with two chains for each pair that repeat the same measurement as a check on each other. The figure covers the pairs within a spin sector at the final step of the seed-11 runs of Li to F, since pairs in different sectors are orthogonal by spin symmetry. Each chain has 2,0482{,}048 walkers and runs 5,0005{,}000 steps of burn-in and up to 10510^{5} steps. The standard error of each estimate is computed by resampling the walkers, each with its whole trajectory, which accounts for the correlation along a stationary chain.

Table 4 classes each pair by whether its two long chains agree and are long enough: converged when they agree within three combined standard errors, every integrated autocorrelation time τint\tau_{\mathrm{int}} is resolved, and each chain is at least 50​τint50\,\tau_{\mathrm{int}} long; short when only the last condition fails; differ when the chains differ by three combined standard errors or more; and unresolved when a τint\tau_{\mathrm{int}} window reaches the end of its chain. A chain shorter than 50​τint50\,\tau_{\mathrm{int}} was extended once, except on F.

Appendix G Implementation details

Every choice in this section keeps the eigenfunctions of 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H} and changes how training reaches them. Appendix F gives the Monte Carlo estimates of energies and overlaps.

G.1 The per-network shifted operator

The weight from the analytic solve.

The overlap-term weights λℓ\lambda_{\ell} of gkg_{k} under the shifted operator 𝒯𝓀=ℰref,𝓀​ℐ−ℋ\mathpzc{T}_{k}=E_{\mathrm{ref},k}\mathpzc{I}-\mathpzc{H} follow from the analytic solve of Eq. (6), and one extra triangular solve gives them for all KK networks. The shift adds Eref,kE_{\mathrm{ref},k} to each 𝖱ℓ​ℓ𝒯\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}_{\ell\ell} and leaves 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} unchanged, and the solve is linear in diag(𝖱𝒯)\mathop{\rm diag}\nolimits(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}), so the new weights, the eigenvalue parameters of 𝒯𝓀\mathpzc{T}_{k}, are

𝝀(k)=𝝀⋆+Eref,k𝐮,𝐮:=(𝖨+𝖬𝗌𝖾𝗊⊙(𝖱ℐ⊙(𝖱ℐ)⊺))−1𝟏,\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{(k)}=\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\star}+E_{\mathrm{ref},k}\,\mathbf{u},\qquad\mathbf{u}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\bigl(\mathsf{I}+\mathsf{M}^{\mathsf{seq}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}}\odot(\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}})^{\intercal})\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{1}, (16)

with 𝟏\mathbf{1} the all-ones vector. Network kk uses λℓ(k)\lambda^{(k)}_{\ell} in place of λℓ\lambda_{\ell} in gk​(𝐱)g_{k}({\bf x}). When the overlaps between networks vanish, 𝐮=𝟏\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{1}. With the prefactor λk\lambda_{k} dropped, the shift adds the constant −Eref,k-E_{\mathrm{ref},k} to the energy term of gk​(𝐱)g_{k}({\bf x}), which cancels in the centered gradient, so only the weights of the overlap term change.

Controlled experiment on carbon.

The shift lowers the curvature of a carbon D1{}^{1}\!D network toward the lower levels from about 724724 times the smaller curvature outside the level to at most 1717 times it, which stabilizes the energy convergence (Section 4.4). For a network of the D1{}^{1}\!D level other than the first in order, the smaller curvature outside the level is the D1{}^{1}\!D–S1{}^{1}\!S gap of 52.252.2 mHa [32]. The first has no lower network in its spin sector, so the shift does not change its curvatures. With 𝒯=−ℋ\mathpzc{T}=-\mathpzc{H}, that is Eref,k=0E_{\mathrm{ref},k}=0, the curvature toward the lower levels is Ek≈37.8\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}E_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\approx 37.8 Ha, so the ratio κ\kappa of this curvature to the gap is about 724724; with Eref,k=−λk+c​σkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}=-\lambda_{k}+c\,\sigma_{k} at c=5c=5 it is c​σk≲0.87c\,\sigma_{k}\lesssim 0.87 Ha on the seed-11 carbon run of Table 2 after step 15,00015{,}000, above the gap, so κ≲17\kappa\lesssim 17.

Weight floor.

At an exact eigenstate, −λk=Ek-\lambda_{k}=E_{k} and σk=0\sigma_{k}=0, so Eref,k=EkE_{\mathrm{ref},k}=E_{k} and the lower-state curvature vanishes. A trained network is an approximate eigenstate, so in practice σk\sigma_{k} stays positive. In theory, if Eℓ=EkE_{\ell}=E_{k} for some ℓ<k\ell<k, the weight λℓ(k)=Eref,k−Eℓ\lambda^{(k)}_{\ell}=E_{\mathrm{ref},k}-E_{\ell} is c​σk=0c\,\sigma_{k}=0, and a rotation of ψk\psi_{k} toward ψℓ\psi_{\ell} within their level keeps σk=0\sigma_{k}=0, so the objective leaves their overlap free. This case arises only at an exact eigenstate, outside the practical regime, and as a guard the implementation replaces every weight λℓ(k)\lambda^{(k)}_{\ell} of Eq. (16) by max⁡(λℓ(k),1​mHa)\max(\lambda^{(k)}_{\ell},1\,\mathrm{mHa}).

G.2 State ordering

Within each spin sector we permute the order indices of the networks at every step, ranking the networks by the EMA (Appendix F) of each network’s batch mean of ℰk+S^loc2\mathcal{E}_{k}+\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}, taken before clipping (Appendix G.3). The EMAs of 𝖱𝒯\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}}, 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} and the norm ratios are kept per network, and the eigenvalue solve permutes 𝖱𝒯\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{T}} and 𝖱ℐ\mathsf{R}^{\mathpzc{I}} into the step’s order. At the fixed point of Corollary D.1 the local energies are constant and the networks are already in energy order, so the assignment leaves the fixed point unchanged; within a degenerate level the order is free, as the corollary allows. After step 10,00010{,}000, in our runs of Li to F, the assignment changes between networks that end in different levels in three runs: on one Li seed the networks of the 3​p3p P∘2{}^{2}\!P^{\circ} and 3​d3d D2{}^{2}\!D levels swap near step 17,00017{,}000, and on two B seeds two networks swap within the 3​p3p P∘2{}^{2}\!P^{\circ} level until one of them descends to the D2{}^{2}\!D level.

G.3 Spin penalty

The spin penalty replaces the operator −ℋ-\mathpzc{H} of the Hilbert–Schmidt objective by −(ℋ+𝒮^2)-(\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2}), which keeps the eigenstates and raises each level of total spin SS by S⁡(S+1)S(S{+}1). The molecular Hamiltonian commutes with S^2\hat{S}^{2} for spin-independent (Coulomb) interactions, so ℋ\mathpzc{H} and ℋ+𝒮^2\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2} share an eigenbasis.

In NestedLoRA-VMC, gkg_{k} in Eq. (5) replaces 𝒯​ψ𝓀/ψ𝓀\mathpzc{T}\psi_{k}/\psi_{k} with the augmented local quantity:

(ℋ+𝒮^2)​ψ𝓀​(𝐱)ψk​(𝐱)=ℰk​(𝐱)+S^loc2​(𝐱).\displaystyle\frac{(\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2})\psi_{k}({\bf x})}{\psi_{k}({\bf x})}=\mathcal{E}_{k}({\bf x})+\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\bf x}).

The local spin S^loc2\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} is evaluated by the Löwdin swap-ratio formula on the same MCMC sample 𝐱{\bf x} (Eq. 44 of Pfau et al. [27]). For n↑≥n↓n_{\uparrow}\geq n_{\downarrow} up- and down-spin electrons, the Löwdin formula is:

S^loc2(𝐱)=mS(mS+1)+n↓−∑i∈↑,j∈↓ψk​(τi​j​𝐱)ψk​(𝐱),\displaystyle\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}({\bf x})=m_{S}(m_{S}{+}1)+n_{\downarrow}-\sum_{i\in\uparrow,\,j\in\downarrow}\frac{\psi_{k}(\tau_{ij}{\bf x})}{\psi_{k}({\bf x})},

where τi​j\tau_{ij} exchanges the positions of up-spin electron ii and down-spin electron jj.

Because both local quantities are evaluated on identical walkers, the per-walker sum ℰk+S^loc2\mathcal{E}_{k}+\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} is the local energy of ℋ+𝒮^2\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2}, and we clip this sum as one quantity with the window of Appendix F.1 (as the NES-VMC implementation does [34]). Clipping ℰk\mathcal{E}_{k} alone and subtracting a separate batch-mean ⟨S^2⟩\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle would leave the heavy tails of S^loc2\hat{S}^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}} unclipped.

We add S^2\hat{S}^{2} to the operator in the run of every atom, in one mSm_{S} sector per spin multiplicity (Appendix H.4), so the penalty enters only the KK local quantities gkg_{k}, one for each network. Szabó et al. [37] instead add the penalty to the loss as a separate term (Appendix C.2), and NES-VMC [27] adds a multiple of S^2\hat{S}^{2} to the Hamiltonian for the singlet states of cyclopentadienone and tetrazine, where the penalty enters all K2K^{2} entries of its local-energy matrix.

Appendix H Experimental setup details

This section gives the settings of the runs reported in Section 4.1. Each network ψk\psi_{k} is a Psiformer (Appendix H.1), and we discuss its computational stability in float32 (Appendix H.1.1). Each network samples its own walkers by Metropolis steps (Appendix H.2) and is optimized by natural gradient descent with KFAC (Appendix H.3). The per-atom settings give the spin sectors, the terms each sector holds and the CASSCF active space (Appendix H.4), and pretraining fits each network to one root of the CASSCF (Appendix H.5). With the envelope shift, the local energies, log⁡ψk\log\psi_{k} and updates of the reported runs stayed finite, and non-finite values that could later occur are handled by dropping the affected walkers and undoing the affected steps (Appendix H.6).

H.1 Architectures

All experiments use Psiformer [38] in the DeepQMC framework [9]; each per-state ansatz ψk\psi_{k} in our NestedLoRA-VMC method is an independent Psiformer instance. As in FermiNet [26], each network has two stages: a permutation-equivariant backbone computes one feature vector per electron, and orbitals obtained from these features by a linear map enter determinants, which make ψk\psi_{k} antisymmetric.

Permutation-equivariant backbones.

Each layer of the Psiformer or FermiNet backbone updates the feature of an electron from its own feature and from the unordered set of the features of all electrons, so permuting the electrons permutes the features in the same way. In the Psiformer each layer is a self-attention over all electrons followed by an MLP [38], and in FermiNet each layer appends to the feature of an electron the means of the one- and two-electron features over the electrons of each spin [26].

Our Psiformer instance has four self-attention layers, four heads and MLP hidden dimension 256256 (Table 5). Relative to the reference implementation [34], the DeepQMC Psiformer omits the layer normalization after each residual sum.

Orbitals and determinants.

The second stage completes the antisymmetry: orbitals computed by a linear map from the feature of electron ii fill row ii of each determinant detAd\det A_{d}, so the exchange of two electrons of the same spin swaps two rows of every determinant and changes the sign of ψk\psi_{k}, and every network therefore lies in ℋ\mathscr{H}. Figure 5 shows the detailed structure.

Each network is ψ=eJ​∑d=1ndetdetAd\psi=e^{J}\sum_{d=1}^{n_{\det}}\det A_{d} with a Jastrow factor eJe^{J} symmetric in the electrons and Slater matrices

Ad=(ϕd​1​(𝐫1)⋯ϕd​n𝖾𝗅​(𝐫1)ϕd​1​(𝐫n𝖾𝗅)⋯ϕd​n𝖾𝗅​(𝐫n𝖾𝗅)),ϕd​j​(𝐫i)=fd​i​j​∑I=1n𝗇𝗎πd​j​Iσi​exp⁡(−ed​i​j​I),A_{d}=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{d1}(\mathbf{r}_{1})&\cdots&\phi_{d{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}(\mathbf{r}_{1})\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ \phi_{d1}(\mathbf{r}_{{n_{\mathsf{el}}}})&\cdots&\phi_{d{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}(\mathbf{r}_{{n_{\mathsf{el}}}})\end{pmatrix},\qquad\phi_{dj}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=f_{dij}\sum_{I=1}^{{n_{\mathsf{nu}}}}\pi^{\sigma_{i}}_{djI}\exp(-e_{dijI}),

with exponents ed​i​j​I=ζd​j​Iσi​‖𝐫i−𝐑I‖e_{dijI}=\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\zeta^{\sigma_{i}}_{djI}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\,\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}\|. Row i∈[n𝖾𝗅]i\in[{n_{\mathsf{el}}}] holds the orbitals j∈[n𝖾𝗅]j\in[{n_{\mathsf{el}}}] at electron ii. The index d∈[ndet]d\in[n_{\det}] runs over the determinants and I∈[n𝗇𝗎]I\in[{n_{\mathsf{nu}}}] over the nuclei. Each orbital is the network output fd​i​jf_{dij} times the envelope ∑Iπd​j​Iσi​exp⁡(−ed​i​j​I)\sum_{I}\pi^{\sigma_{i}}_{djI}\exp(-e_{dijI}). The output fd​i​jf_{dij} depends on all electrons. The envelope parameters πd​j​Iσ\pi^{\sigma}_{djI} and ζd​j​Iσ\zeta^{\sigma}_{djI} are trained for each spin σ\sigma and taken at the spin σi\sigma_{i} of electron ii.

H.1.1 Computational stability

Below we discuss the issues that can arise in float32 from the envelopes and from the derivative of the electron–nucleus distance, together with their solutions.

Envelope underflow.

We keep log⁡ψ\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} and its derivatives finite in float32 by shifting the exponents in each row of the Slater matrix AdA_{d} above, a shift that leaves them exact. If a row of the shifted matrix A~d\tilde{A}_{d} still has largest absolute entry below the smallest normal float32 value 1.2×10−381.2\times 10^{-38}, its precision is lost and we set detAd\det A_{d} and its derivative to zero. Each entry of AdA_{d} is the network output fd​i​jf_{dij} times an envelope that decays exponentially in the distance of electron ii from the nuclei, so without the shift the entries of an electron far from every nucleus are stored as zero and the derivative of log⁡ψ\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} becomes non-finite.

Consider an electron ii far from every nucleus, so that every exponent ed​i​j​Ie_{dijI} is large. Each term exp⁡(−ed​i​j​I)\exp(-e_{dijI}) falls below 1.2×10−381.2\times 10^{-38} once ed​i​j​I≳87e_{dijI}\gtrsim 87 and is stored as zero once ed​i​j​I≳103e_{dijI}\gtrsim 103, so row ii is zero or subnormal in some or all AdA_{d}. The derivative of logdetAd\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\det A_{d}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} is the transposed inverse (Ad−1)⊤(A_{d}^{-1})^{\top}, and the inverse of a matrix with a zero or subnormal row is non-finite. A determinant that contributes nothing to ψ\psi still passes this value on, because its zero weight multiplies a non-finite derivative.

We subtract the smallest exponent in row ii of AdA_{d}, cd​i=minj,I⁡ed​i​j​Ic_{di}=\min_{j,I}e_{dijI}, from every exponent ed​i​j​Ie_{dijI} of that row (Figure 5). This multiplies row ii by ecd​ie^{c_{di}} and gives the shifted matrix A~d\tilde{A}_{d}, whose largest exponential in row ii is exp⁡(0)=1\exp(0)=1. The shift is the subtract-max trick of the softmax applied to the logits −ed​i​j​I-e_{dijI}, whose largest value is −cd​i-c_{di}, and it leaves log⁡ψ\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} and its derivatives exact. In the softmax the trick prevents overflow of large logits; here every logit −ed​i​j​I-e_{dijI} is at most zero, and for a distant electron the largest one, −cd​i-c_{di}, is large and negative, so the subtraction raises every entry of row ii and prevents underflow.

A determinant is linear in each row, so logdetAd=logdetA~d−∑icd​i\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\det A_{d}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}=\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\det\tilde{A}_{d}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}-\sum_{i}c_{di} for every value of cd​ic_{di}. We compute logdetA~d\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\det\tilde{A}_{d}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} from rows stored at full precision and subtract ∑icd​i\sum_{i}c_{di} before the determinants are summed. Since the identity holds for every cd​ic_{di}, we hold cd​ic_{di} constant under differentiation. A second subtract-max, over the determinants instead of the entries of a row, sums the determinants:

xd=logdetA~d−∑i=1n𝖾𝗅cd​i,M=maxdxd,logψ=J+M+log∑d=1ndetsgn(detA~d)exd−M.x_{d}=\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\det\tilde{A}_{d}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}-\sum_{i=1}^{{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}c_{di},\quad M=\max_{d}x_{d},\quad\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}=J+M+\log\Bigl\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\sum_{d=1}^{n_{\det}}\mathrm{sgn}(\det\tilde{A}_{d})\,e^{x_{d}-M}\Bigr\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}.

The first shift keeps the entries of A~d\tilde{A}_{d} from underflowing, and the second keeps the terms exde^{x_{d}} of the sum, lowered by ∑icd​i\sum_{i}c_{di}, from underflowing.

Safe norm of the electron–nucleus distance.

The reported runs were trained with the safe norm ρ=r2+a2\rho=\sqrt{r^{2}+a^{2}} of the DeepQMC code [9], where a2a^{2} is the float32 machine epsilon (a=3.45×10−4a=3.45\times 10^{-4} bohr), in place of each electron–nucleus distance r=‖𝐫i−𝐑I‖r=\|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}\| in the exponents of the envelopes and in the input features. This helps with the undefined derivative (𝐫i−𝐑I)/r(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I})/r of rr where rr vanishes, since that of ρ\rho is finite everywhere.

While this choice may be numerically stable, it also induces rare jumps of the local energy, and the reported energies evaluate the network and the local energy with exact interparticle distances (Appendix J), which removes these jumps. The potential −Z/r-Z/r takes the exact distance rr, so within about aa of a nucleus the safe norm breaks the cancellation between the kinetic energy and the nuclear Coulomb term. For an envelope e−ζ​ρe^{-\zeta\rho}, the term −∂rψ/(rψ)-\mathop{}\!\partial_{r}\psi/(r\psi) of the kinetic energy equals ζ/ρ\zeta/\rho and is at most ζ/a\zeta/a, whereas for e−ζ​re^{-\zeta r} it equals ζ/r\zeta/r and cancels −Z/r-Z/r at the nuclear cusp when ζ=Z\zeta=Z. A walker with an electron within about aa of a nucleus thus has a local energy far below its value with exact distances, which makes the unclipped batch mean of the local energy jump at the step that samples it.

We conjecture that training with the exact distance rr removes these jumps and gives more accurate energies, since the envelopes then keep this cancellation at every distance from a nucleus. We also suspect that the safe norm is a broader precaution than the computation needs, because the FermiNet code [34] keeps the exact electron–nucleus distance and masks only the difference of each electron with itself, and the same mask appears applicable here.

H.2 Samplers

The training chains follow the Metropolis sampler of DeepQMC v1.2.0 [9, 33]: each network ψk\psi_{k} has its own chain of 4,0964{,}096 walkers, which samples pkp_{k} (Section 4.1). A proposal moves all electrons of a walker by a Gaussian step of width τ\tau and is accepted with probability min⁡{1,ψk​(𝐱′)2/ψk​(𝐱)2}\min\{1,\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}({\bf x}^{\prime})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}/\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}({\bf x})\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}\}. Each training step takes 3030 Metropolis steps, and after each Metropolis step τ\tau is multiplied by max⁡(aacc,0.05)/0.57\max(a_{\mathrm{acc}},0.05)/0.57, where aacca_{\mathrm{acc}} is the acceptance rate over the walkers of the chain; τ\tau starts at 11 bohr. The chains start from the walkers at the end of pretraining and are equilibrated under the pretrained networks before training.

H.3 Natural-gradient descent with KFAC

Optimization uses per-state natural gradient descent: each per-state gradient is left-multiplied by the inverse Fisher information Fk−1F_{k}^{-1}, with

Fk:=𝔼pk[∇θlogpk(𝐱)∇θlogpk(𝐱)⊺].\displaystyle F_{k}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{k}({\bf x})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{k}({\bf x})^{\intercal}].

The parameter update direction is

Δ​θ=2​∑k=1KFk−1​𝔼pk​(𝐱)​[(gk​(𝐱)−𝔼pk​[gk])​∇θ​log⁡ψk].\displaystyle\Delta\theta=2\sum_{k=1}^{K}F_{k}^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}({\bf x})}\!\bigl[(g_{k}({\bf x})-\mathbb{E}_{p_{k}}[g_{k}])\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\bigr]. (17)

In practice each FkF_{k} is approximated by KFAC [21], applied per state. The factorization by state holds because each network samples its own Born density (Section 3.4): the walkers 𝐱∼pk{\bf x}\sim p_{k} enter only FkF_{k}, so the KFAC blocks decouple across kk.

Hyperparameters.

The optimizer uses an inverse-time learning-rate schedule ηn=0.05/(1+n/5×104)\eta_{n}=0.05/(1+n/5\times 10^{4}). KFAC-specific settings: norm constraint 10−310^{-3}, constant damping 10−310^{-3}, Fisher factors computed exactly from the registered output log⁡ψk\log\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} rather than from sampled targets, inverse update period 11, no burn-in. The norm constraint is applied to each spin sector separately: the update of the networks of a sector is multiplied by min⁡{1,(10−3/(ηn2​G))1/2}\min\{1,(10^{-3}/(\eta_{n}^{2}G))^{1/2}\}, where GG is the sum over the networks of that sector of the inner product of each network’s preconditioned gradient with its gradient.

H.4 Per-atom setup

Sector decision.

Every atom runs NestedLoRA-VMC on 𝒯=−(ℋ+𝒮^2)\mathpzc{T}=-(\mathpzc{H}+\hat{S}^{2}) in one mSm_{S} sector per spin multiplicity, and the states of all sectors are merged by energy (Section 4.1). The augmented Hamiltonian shifts each state by S⁡(S+1)S(S{+}1) Ha. This shift differs by at least 22 Ha between two values of SS in one sector, far above the excitation energies in the K=10K{=}10 window (Table 9), so a single-sector run with the spin penalty would lift every state with S>mSS>\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}m_{S}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{} out of the K=10K{=}10 window. One mSm_{S} sector per spin multiplicity is also the recipe of Szabó et al. [37] (their Section 2.1.3), who fix mSm_{S} to reach each higher spin multiplicity and keep the spin penalty on.

H.5 Pretraining

Per-state CASSCF targets.

Network kk of a sector is pretrained to the leading determinants of the kk-th root of the sector’s state-averaged CASSCF.

Pretraining sampler.

As in FermiNet’s excited-state pretraining [34], each state’s pretraining walkers come from a chain on the density of its CASSCF reference that continues from one iteration to the next, whereas the penalty baseline [37] restarts its chains at every iteration.

Optimization.

The pretrain loss is the mean-squared error between the network orbital matrices and the per-state CASSCF target. We optimize with Lamb at learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} (β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}{=}0.999) for 10,00010{,}000 steps in all reported runs.

H.6 NaN handling in training

A non-finite log⁡ψk\log\psi_{k}, local energy or cross-state ratio at a single walker makes every batch mean it enters non-finite. A non-finite update then leaves the parameters non-finite at every later step. Although the reported runs kept log⁡ψk\log\psi_{k}, the local energy and the parameters finite with the envelope shift of Appendix H.1.1, we adopt two safeguards from the NES-VMC stability handler of Pfau et al. [27, Section S8]. (i) Per-walker exclusion: any walker with non-finite log⁡ψk\log\psi_{k}, local energy or cross-state ratio is dropped from every batch reduction in gkg_{k}, including the analytic-eigenvalue solver inputs and the EMAs. (ii) Step undo with a failure counter: a step that leaves the parameters, the optimizer state or the statistics fed back to the next step non-finite is undone, as FermiNet does [34]. A step with a non-finite walker or an undone update increments a counter of consecutive failures, and at 100100 the run restarts from its last checkpoint. The other two safeguards of that handler address the joint matrix of NES-VMC and larger systems. Extra MCMC on zero entries ψi​(𝐱j)\psi_{i}({\bf x}^{j}) treats a sparse joint matrix with nonzero detΨ\det\Psi. In NestedLoRA-VMC each network kk samples its walkers from ψk2\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{k}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}, so ψk\psi_{k} is nonzero at every one of them. The median-of-minibatches energy estimator was introduced for systems with >25>25 electrons, beyond the first-row atoms studied here.

Appendix I Per-step cost analysis

NestedLoRA-VMC evaluates KK Laplacians per training step and NES-VMC evaluates K2K^{2}. This section counts the cost of one step for both methods and measures the wall time of NestedLoRA-VMC on Ne as KK grows.

One forward evaluation of a network costs 𝒞eval=𝒞bb+𝒞post\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}}=\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{bb}}+\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{post}}, the sum over the two stages of Appendix H.1, with 𝒞bb∼n𝖾𝗅2\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{bb}}\sim{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{2} and 𝒞post∼n𝖾𝗅3\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{post}}\sim{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{3} at fixed depth and width. The backbone of a network is its permutation-equivariant layers, of order n𝖾𝗅2{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{2} from the self-attention of Psiformer or the symmetric features of FermiNet. The orbitals, envelopes and determinants of one state have the order n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{3} from the determinants. A Laplacian costs 𝒞lap∼3​n𝖾𝗅​𝒞eval∼n𝖾𝗅4\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{lap}}\sim 3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}}\sim{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{4} (Appendix I.1). A training step takes nMH=30n_{\mathrm{MH}}=30 Metropolis steps (Appendix H.2).

I.1 Forward-Laplacian primitive (folx)

We compute every Laplacian Δ​f=∑k=13​n𝖾𝗅⁡∂2f/⁡∂⁡xk2\Delta f=\sum_{k=1}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}}\mathop{}\!\partial^{2}f/\mathop{}\!\partial x_{k}^{2} with the forward Laplacian of folx [5], at about half the cost of the standard Hessian-diagonal loop. DeepQMC [9] and FermiNet [34] by default run 3​n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}} forward-mode Jacobian–vector products through the gradient ∇𝐱f\nabla_{\bf x}f, each about one forward and one backward pass, ∼2⋅3​n𝖾𝗅​𝒞eval\sim 2\cdot 3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}} in total. The forward Laplacian instead propagates (h,∇h,Δ​h)(h,\nabla h,\Delta h) with ∇h∈ℝ3​n𝖾𝗅×dl\nabla h\in\mathbb{R}^{3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\times d_{l}} through the network in one pass, and the Jacobian products (3​n𝖾𝗅×dl)⋅(dl×dl+1)(3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\times d_{l})\cdot(d_{l}\times d_{l+1}) of its layers sum to 𝒞lap∼3​n𝖾𝗅​𝒞eval\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{lap}}\sim 3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}}.

The sparse mode of folx shrinks the Jacobian to (s×dl)(s\times d_{l}) in layers whose outputs depend on at most ss input coordinates, which holds with s=3s=3 only in the leading per-electron embedding and MLP. From the first self-attention of Psiformer [38] or the first mean over electrons of FermiNet [26] on, the features of an electron depend on all 3​n𝖾𝗅3{n_{\mathsf{el}}} coordinates, so the Laplacian cost stays at ∼3​n𝖾𝗅​𝒞eval\sim 3{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}}.

I.2 Cost decomposition: Hamiltonian coupling and ansatz parameterization

Table 7 counts every component of a step under the two ansatz parameterizations, a joint backbone with KK heads and KK disjoint networks.

Hamiltonian coupling: off-diagonal Laplacian count.

The K2K^{2} Laplacians of NES-VMC come from its local-energy matrix 𝖤𝗅𝗈𝖼​(𝐗)=Ψ​(𝐗)−1​(ℋ​Ψ)​(𝐗)\mathsf{E}_{\mathsf{loc}}({\bf X})=\Psi({\bf X})^{-1}(\mathpzc{H}\Psi)({\bf X}), which contains (ℋ​ψ𝓀)​(𝐱𝒾)(\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k})({\bf x}^{i}) at every state-walker pair (i,k)(i,k). In NestedLoRA-VMC and the penalty methods the cross term is the overlap ⟨ψk​ψℓ⟩\langle\psi_{k}~\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}~\psi_{\ell}\rangle, a forward-only evaluation, so only the KK diagonal local energies ℋ​ψ𝓀/ψ𝓀\mathpzc{H}\psi_{k}/\psi_{k} need a Laplacian, a factor KK fewer than NES-VMC. The inverse Ψ−1\Psi^{-1} and the product Ψ−1​(ℋ​Ψ)\Psi^{-1}(\mathpzc{H}\Psi) add O⁡(K3)O(K^{3}) per step to NES-VMC, below its Laplacian cost K2​n𝖾𝗅4K^{2}{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{4} for n𝖾𝗅≳K{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\gtrsim K.

Ansatz parameterization and walker-target factorization.

The parameterization changes the overlap term of NestedLoRA-VMC, and the Laplacian and sampling terms of NES-VMC. The walker target ψ12⋯ψK2\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{1}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2}\cdots\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\psi_{K}\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2} of NestedLoRA-VMC and the penalty methods factorizes into KK Markov chains, so sampling and Laplacians evaluate each network at its own walkers under either parameterization. The overlaps evaluate every network at every walker set, at K2​𝒞postK^{2}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{post}} with a joint backbone, whose KK heads share the backbone features of a walker set, and at K2​𝒞evalK^{2}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}} with the KK disjoint networks that NestedLoRA-VMC uses, following Szabó et al. [37]. The target detΨ2\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}\det\Psi\mathchoice{\mspace{1mu}\mspace{1mu}}{}{}{}^{2} of NES-VMC couples the KK walker sets, so its sampling and Laplacians evaluate the full matrix Ψ⁡(𝐗)\Psi({\bf X}), at K​𝒞bb+K2​𝒞postK\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{bb}}+K^{2}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{post}} with a joint backbone, as in the NES-VMC reference implementation [34], and at K2​𝒞evalK^{2}\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{eval}} with disjoint networks.

Cost of the spin penalty.

For the first-row atoms, with n𝖾𝗅≤10{n_{\mathsf{el}}}\leq 10, the Löwdin sum of Appendix G.3 costs less than the KK Laplacians of a step and much less than the K⁡(K−1)K(K-1) Laplacians that NestedLoRA-VMC saves against NES-VMC. Each of its n↑​n↓n_{\uparrow}n_{\downarrow} terms is one forward evaluation of ψk\psi_{k}, because every orbital of the Psiformer depends on all electron positions. Evaluated at every walker, it adds K​n↑​n↓≤K​n𝖾𝗅2/4Kn_{\uparrow}n_{\downarrow}\leq K{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{2}/4 forward evaluations per walker and step to the forward counts of Table 7, of order K​n𝖾𝗅5K{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{5} against the order K​n𝖾𝗅4K{n_{\mathsf{el}}}^{4} of the Laplacians.

In larger systems the spin term can therefore cost more than the Laplacians, but a small random subsample of the walkers suffices to estimate it, because the eigenvalues S⁡(S+1)S(S+1) of neighboring spin sectors differ by at least 22, far above the excitation energies. Evaluating the spin term on a random eighth of the walkers keeps its cost below that of the Laplacians up to about a hundred electrons, n𝖾𝗅<96{n_{\mathsf{el}}}<96. On Ne, training with the spin term on a random eighth of the walkers reached the same accuracy as training with it on every walker.

I.3 Empirical wall-time scaling on Ne

We confirm the scaling in KK claimed in Section 3.4 by sweeping KK on Ne. Measurements run on a single host with 8×8{\times} RTX 5090 (FP32, JAX 0.9.2). For each value of KK we run 100 main-loop warm-up steps followed by 100 measurement steps. The sweep places all KK networks in one spin sector and runs the training step with the spin penalty off. With two or more sectors, overlaps are evaluated only between networks of the same sector, and the spin penalty adds the cost given in Appendix I.2. Figure 6 reports two batch sizes. At the training batch of 4,0964{,}096 the walkers no longer fit in memory beyond K=24K{=}24. The exponent fitted at this batch in Figure 6 has standard error 0.020.02 (95%95\% interval ±0.04\pm 0.04) and describes the measured range K=6K{=}6 to 2424 on this host.

Appendix J Per-state errors across first-row atoms

This section reports the per-state errors behind the per-atom mean absolute error (MAE, in mHa) of Table 2, for NestedLoRA-VMC, NES-VMC, and Szabó et al. [37] against (2​J+1)(2J{+}1)-weighted NIST term centroids on each of the eight first-row atoms at K=10K{=}10. Table 9 gives the per-state breakdown of one run per atom, whose MAE is in Table 8.

Per-state stderr and MAE interval.

Each per-state energy EkE_{k} is the unweighted mean of the per-state batch mean of the local energy over training steps 97,00097{,}000 to 99,99999{,}999, and its stderr is the standard deviation of the means of 1010 contiguous blocks of 300300 steps, divided by 10\sqrt{10}. For Ne seed 11, read at step 99,00099{,}000, the mean runs over steps 97,00097{,}000 to 98,99998{,}999 and the stderr uses its last 66 blocks of 300300 steps. The local energy is unclipped and is evaluated on each step’s walkers with exact interparticle distances (Appendix H.1). Blocks of 100100 steps give the same stderr: over the states of the runs in Table 2, the ratio of the 1010-block stderr to the 3030-block stderr has median 1.001.00, within the precision of a standard deviation estimated from 1010 blocks.

The interval of the MAE comes from a block bootstrap, because the sampling error of the anchor E1E_{1} enters every per-state error εk=(Ek−E1)−tk\varepsilon_{k}=(E_{k}-E_{1})-t_{k}, with tkt_{k} the target excitation energy. Each of 4,0004{,}000 resamples draws the blocks with replacement, the same blocks for every state, and recomputes the MAE from the resampled per-state means: it sorts them, subtracts the lowest and scores the excitations against the targets tkt_{k}. The 95%95\% interval runs from the 2.52.5th to the 97.597.5th percentile of the resampled MAE. Table 8 gives the interval of every run in Table 2; blocks of 100100 and of 300300 steps give nearly the same interval. The interval measures the sampling noise of one run, and on B it is narrower than the spread across the three seeds.

B: tenth state.

On B, the tenth states of NestedLoRA-VMC and of NES-VMC lie near the 2​s2​3​p2s^{2}3p P∘2{}^{2}\!P^{\circ} level (Δ​ENIST=0.22145\Delta E_{\text{NIST}}=0.22145 Ha), not at a third D2{}^{2}\!D substate. The k=10k{=}10 row of Table 9 scores both against the D2{}^{2}\!D centroid.

Appendix K Compute resources and asset licenses

Compute resources.

Each run of Table 2 trains for 100,000100{,}000 KFAC steps at an electron batch of 4,0964{,}096 on one to four NVIDIA V100 (SXM2, 3232 GB), two NVIDIA A40, or four NVIDIA H100 NVL. A training step took 2.82.8 to 9.39.3 s, depending on the atom and the cards, and these runs took over 3,6003{,}600 GPU-hours, estimated as the per-step time times the number of steps and cards. CASSCF pretraining of Ne took 4747 minutes on four H100 NVL and 140140 minutes on two A40. Preliminary work used about 2,8802{,}880 A6000-hours and 2,8802{,}880 A100-hours. The wall-time sweep of Appendix I.3 ran on one host with 8×8{\times} RTX 5090.
